p.seg: Dìjì Dìyī Shénwǔ Shàng
Qí Gāozǔ Shénwǔ Huángdì,
xìng Gāo míng Huān,
zì Hèlùhún,
Bóhǎi Xiū rén yě.
Liùshìzǔ Yǐn,
Jìn Xuántú Tàishǒu.
Yǐn shēng Qìng,
Qìng shēng Tài,
Tài shēng Hú,
sānshì shì Mùróng shì.
Jí Mùróng Bǎo bài,
guó luàn,
Hú shuài zhòng guī Wèi,
wèi Yòujiāngjūn.
Hú shēng sì zǐ,
dìsān zǐ Mì,
shì Wèi wèizhì Shìyùshǐ,
zuòfǎ xǐjū Huáisuò Zhèn.
Mì shēng Huángkǎo Shù,
xìng tōngshuài,
bù shì jiāyè.
Zhùjū Báidào Nán,
shù yǒu chìguāng zǐqì zhī yì,
línrén yǐwéi guài,
quàn xǐjū yǐ bì zhī.
Huángkǎo yuē:
“Ān zhī fēi jí?”
Jū zhī zìruò.
Jí Shénwǔ shēng ér Huángbǐ Hán shì zū,
yǎng yú tóngchǎn jiěxù Zhènyù Duìwèi Jǐng jiā.
Shénwǔ jì lěishì běibiān,
gù xí qí sú,
suì tóng Xiānbēi.
Zhǎng ér shēncén yǒu dàdù,
qīngcái zhòngshì,
wèi háoxiá suǒ zōng.
Mù yǒu jīngguāng,
chángtóu gāoquán,
chǐ bái rú yù,
shǎo yǒu rénjié biǎo.
Jiā pín,
jí pìn Wǔmíng Huánghòu,
shǐ yǒu mǎ,
dé gěi zhèn wèi Duìzhǔ.
Zhènjiàng Liáoxī Duàn Cháng cháng qí Shénwǔ mào,
wèi yuē:
“Jūn yǒu kāngjì cái,
zhōng bù túrán.”
Biàn yǐ zǐsūn wèi tuō.
Jí guì,
zhuīzèng Cháng Sīkōng,
zhuó qí zǐ Níng yòng zhī.
Shénwǔ zì Duìzhǔ zhuǎn wèi Hánshǐ.
Cháng chéng yì guò Jiànxīng,
yúnwù zhòuhuì,
léishēng suí zhī,
bànhùn nǎi jué,
ruò yǒu shényìng zhě.
Měi xíng dàolù,
wǎnglái wú fēngchén zhī sè.
Yòu cháng mèng lǚ zhòng xīng ér xíng,
jué ér nèixǐ.
Wèi Hánshǐ liù nián,
měi zhì Luòyáng,
gěi Lìngshǐ Má Xiáng shǐ.
Xiáng cháng yǐ ròu dàn Shénwǔ,
Shénwǔ xìng bù lìshí,
zuò ér jìn zhī.
Xiáng yǐwéi màn jǐ,
chī Shénwǔ sìshí.
Jí zì Luòyáng huán,
qīngchǎn yǐ jiékè,
qīn gù guàiwèn zhī.
Dá yuē:
“Wú zhì Luòyáng,
sùwèi yǔlín xiāngshuài fén Lǐngjūn Zhāng Yí zhái,
cháotíng jù qí luàn ér bù wèn,
wèizhèng ruò cǐ,
shì kě zhī yě.
Cáiwù qǐ kě cháng shǒu xié?”
Zì shì nǎi yǒu chéngqīng tiānxià zhī zhì.
Yǔ Huáisuò Shěngshì Yúnzhōng Sīmǎ Zǐrú jí Xiùróng rén Liú Guì, Zhōngshān rén Jiǎ Xiǎnzhì wèi bēnzǒu zhī yǒu,
Huáisuò Hùcáoshǐ Sūn Téng, Wàibīngshǐ Hóu Jǐng yì xiāng yǒujié.
Liú Guì cháng dé yī báiyīng,
yǔ Shénwǔ jí Wèi Jǐng, Cài Jùn, Zǐrú, Jiǎ Xiǎnzhì děng liè yú Wòyě.
Jiàn yī chìtù,
měi bó zhé yì,
suì zhì Huízé.
Zé zhōng yǒu máowū,
jiāng bēnrù,
yǒu gǒu zì wūzhōng chū,
shì zhī,
yīng tù jù sǐ.
Shénwǔ nù,
yǐ míngdí shè zhī,
gǒu bì.
Wūzhōng yǒu èrrén chū,
chí Shénwǔ jīn shèn jí.
Qí mǔ liǎng mù máng,
yè zhàng hē qí èr zǐ yuē:
“Hé gù chù Dàjiā!”
Chū wèng zhōng jiǔ,
pēng yáng yǐ fàn kè.
Yīn zìyán shàn ànxiàng,
biàn mén zhū rén jiē guì,
ér zhǐhuī jù yóu Shénwǔ.
Yòu yuē:
“Zǐrú lìwèi xiǎn,
zhì bù shànzhōng.”
Fàn jìng chū,
xíng shù lǐ huán,
gēng fǎng zhī,
zé běn wú rénjū,
nǎi xiàng fēirén yě.
Yóu shì zhū rén yì jiā jìngyì.
Xiàochāng Yuánnián,
Róuxuán Zhèn rén Dù Luòzhōu fǎn yú Shànggǔ,
Shénwǔ nǎi yǔ tóngzhì cóng zhī.
Chǒu qí xíngshì,
sī yǔ Wèi Jǐng, Duàn Róng, Cài Jùn tú zhī,
bù guǒ ér táo,
wèi qí qí suǒ zhuī.
Wénxiāng jí Wèi Yǒngxī Hòu jiē yòu,
Wǔmíng Hòu yú niú shàng bàofù zhī.
Wénxiāng lǚ luò niú,
Shénwǔ wāngōng jiāng shè zhī yǐ juéqù.
Hòu hū Róng qiújiù,
lài Róng tòuxià qǔ zhī yǐ miǎn.
Suì bēn Gě Róng,
yòu wáng guī Ěrzhū Róng yú Xiùróng.
Xiān shì,
Liú Guì shì Róng,
shèng yán Shénwǔ měi,
zhì shì shǐ dé jiàn,
yǐ qiáocuì gù,
wèi zhī qí yě.
Guì nǎi wèi Shénwǔ gēngyī,
fù qiú jiàn yān.
Yīn suí Róng zhī,
yǒu èmǎ,
Róng mìng jiǎn zhī.
Shénwǔ nǎi bù jiā jībàn ér jiǎn,
jìng bù tí niè,
yǐ ér qǐ yuē:
“Yù èrén yì rúcǐ mǎ yǐ.”
Róng suì zuò Shénwǔ yú chuángxià,
bìng zuǒyòu ér fǎng shíshì.
Shénwǔ yuē:
“Wén gōng yǒu mǎ shí'èr gǔ,
sè bié wèi qún,
jiāng cǐ jìng hé yòng yě?”
Róng yuē:
“Dàn yán ěr yì.”
Shénwǔ yuē:
“Fāng tiānzǐ yúruò,
Tàihòu yínluàn,
nièchǒng shànmìng,
cháozhèng bù xíng,
yǐ Mínggōng xióngwǔ,
chéngshí fènfā,
tǎo Zhèng Yǎn, Xú Hè ér qīng dì cè,
bàyè kě jǔ biān ér chéng.
Cǐ Hèlùhún zhī yì yě.”
Róng dàyuè,
yǔ zì rìzhōng zhì yèbàn,
nǎi chū.
Zì shì měi cāncān jūn móu.
Hòu cóng Róng xǐ jù Bìngzhōu,
dǐ Yángzhōu yìrén Páng Cāngyīng,
zhǐ tuán jiāo zhōng.
Měi cóng wài guī,
zhǔrén yáowén xíng xiǎng dòngdì.
Cāngyīng mǔ shù jiàn tuán jiāo chìqì hèrán shǔ tiān.
Yòu Cāngyīng cháng yè yù rù,
yǒu qīngyī rén bá dāo chì yuē:
“Hé gù chù Wáng!”
Yán qì bù jiàn.
Shǐ yǐwéi yì,
mì zhān zhī,
wéi jiàn chì shé pán chuáng shàng,
nǎi yì jīngyì.
Yīn shā niú fēnròu,
hòu yǐ xiāng fèng.
Cāngyīng mǔ qiú yǐ Shénwǔ wèi yìzǐ.
Jí dézhì,
yǐ qí zhái wèi dì,
hào wèi Nánzhái.
Suī ménxiàng kāiguǎng,
tángyǔ chónglì,
qí běn suǒ zhù tuán jiāo,
yǐ shí è tú zhī,
liú ér bù huǐ,
zhì Wénxuān shí suì wèi gōng.
Jì ér Róng yǐ Shénwǔ wèi Qīnxìn Dūdū.
In the seventh month,
Wèi Dì (魏帝) personally led a large army to encamp at Héqiáo (河橋).
Shénwǔ (神武) arrived within more than ten *lǐ* (里) of the north bank of the river.
He again sent Kǒushēnchéng (口申誠) to relay a message,
but Wèi Dì did not reply.
Shénwǔ then led his army across the river.
Wèi Dì asked his officials for advice.
Some suggested moving south to join Hèbá Shèng (賀拔勝),
some suggested moving west to Guānzhōng (關中),
and some suggested holding Luòkǒu (洛口) and fighting to the death.
No decision was made.
Meanwhile, Yuán Bīnzhī (元斌之) and Hú Xīs Chūn (斛斯椿) were contending for power and were not on good terms.
Bīnzhī abandoned Chūn and returned directly,
deceiving the Emperor by saying:
"Shénwǔ's troops have arrived."
That very day,
Wèi Dì withdrew to Cháng'ān (長安).
On the *jǐyǒu* day (己酉),
Shénwǔ entered Luòyáng (洛陽)
and stayed at Yǒngníng Sì (永寧寺).
On the *jiǎyín* day (甲寅) of the eighth month,
he summoned all the officials
and said to them:
"As ministers serving their lord,
you should assist in times of crisis and chaos.
If, while in office, you do not remonstrate,
and when abroad, you do not accompany your lord,
but in times of ease you indulge in favor and contend for glory,
and in times of urgency you flee and hide,
where then is the fidelity of a minister!"

Thereupon, he arrested Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司) Chìliè Yánqìng (叱列延慶), concurrently Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè (尚書左僕射) Xīn Xióng (辛雄), concurrently Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書) Cuī Xiàofēn (崔孝芬), Dūguān Shàngshū (都官尚書) Liú Xīn (劉廞), concurrently Dùzhī Shàngshū (度支尚書) Yáng Jī (楊機), and Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) Yuán Shìbì (元士弼), and executed them all,
punishing them for their disloyalty.
Shìbì's family and property were confiscated.
As all affairs of the state could not be neglected,
Shénwǔ discussed with his officials the appointment of Qīnghé Wáng Dǎn (清河王亶) as Dàsīmǎ (大司馬).
He resided in the lower residence of the Shàngshū (尚書) and governed by imperial decree.
The King used imperial escorts (警蹕),
which Shénwǔ disliked.
Shénwǔ soon arrived at Nóng (農),
then captured Tóngguān (潼關) to the west,
and seized Máo Hóngbīn (毛洪賓).
Advancing the army to Chángchéng (長城),
Lóngmén Dūdū (龍門都督) Xuē Chónglǐ (薛崇禮) surrendered.
Shénwǔ withdrew his army to Hédōng (河東),
ordering Xíngtái Shàngshū Zhǎngshǐ (行臺尚書長史) Xuē Yú (薛瑜) to guard Tóngguān (潼關),
and Dàdūdū (大都督) Kùdí Wēn (厙狄溫) to guard Fēnglíng (封陵).
He built a city on the western bank of Pújīn (蒲津),
to guard Huázhōu (華州),
and appointed Xuē Shàozōng (薛紹宗) as Cìshǐ (刺史).
Gāo Áng (高昂) acted as the governor of Yùzhōu (豫州).
From the time Shénwǔ departed from Jìnyáng (晉陽)
until then, there were forty memorials,
but Wèi Dì did not reply to any.
On the *gēngyín* day (庚寅) of the ninth month,
Shénwǔ returned to Luòyáng (洛陽),
and sent Monk Dàoróng (道榮) to deliver a memorial to Guānzhōng (關中),
which again received no reply.
Thereupon, he gathered all the officials and elders from the four gates
to discuss who should be enthroned.
They believed that since the chaos of Xiàochāng (孝昌),
the imperial succession had been interrupted,
the divine lord had no one to rely on,
and the order of generations was lost.
Yǒng'ān (永安) regarded Xiàowén (孝文) as a paternal elder cousin,
and Yǒngxī (永熙) exiled Xiàomíng (孝明) to a side chamber.
The loss of their enterprise and short reigns
were due to these reasons.
They then deliberated on establishing the heir of Qīnghé Wáng (清河王), Shànjiàn (善見).
After the discussion was settled,
they reported to Qīnghé Wáng.
The King said:
"The Son of Heaven has no father;
if my son is to be enthroned,
I will not begrudge my remaining life."
So he was established,
known as Xiàojìng Dì (孝靜帝).
Wèi (魏) thus began to be divided into two.
As Xiàowǔ (孝武) had gone west,
Shénwǔ feared being pressured at Xiáo (崤) and Shǎn (陝),
and Luòyáng (洛陽) was again outside the river,
close to the territory of Liáng (梁).
If he went towards Jìnyáng (晉陽),
the strategic positions could not connect.
Therefore, he discussed moving the capital to Yè (鄴),
and Hùjūn (護軍) Zǔ Yíng (祖瑩) supported it.
Three days after the imperial edict was issued,
the imperial carriage departed,
and 400,000 households rushed to set out in haste.
Shénwǔ remained in Luòyáng (洛陽) to manage affairs,
and returned to Jìnyáng (晉陽) when they were completed.
From then on, all military and state affairs
belonged to the Prime Minister's residence.
Previously, there was a children's rhyme that said:
"Pity the little green sparrow,
flying to Yèchéng (鄴城) to build its nest.
Its wings are almost fully grown,
and it will transform into a little parrot."
Those who favored omens secretly said
that the sparrow referred to Wèi Dì (魏帝) and the son of Qīnghé Wáng (清河王),
and the parrot referred to Shénwǔ (神武).
Initially, during the Xiàochāng (孝昌) era,
the Shānhú (山胡) Liú Líshēng (劉蠡升) proclaimed himself Son of Heaven,
with the era name Shénjiā (神嘉).
He resided in Yúnyáng Gǔ (雲陽谷),
and the western regions were plundered by him every year,
calling it "Hú Wilderness" (胡荒).
In the first month of the second year,
the Western Wèi (西魏) Wèizhōu Cìshǐ (渭州刺史) Kězhūhún Dàoyuán (可朱渾道元) led his followers to defect to them.
Shénwǔ welcomed and accepted him.
On the *rénxū* day (壬戌),
Shénwǔ attacked Liú Líshēng (劉蠡升)
and greatly defeated him.
On the *jǐsì* day (己巳),
Wèi Dì issued an edict of commendation,
appointing Shénwǔ as Xiàngguó (相國),
granting him the *huángyuè* (黃鉞),
permitting him to wear swords and shoes into the palace,
and not requiring him to walk quickly when in court.
Shénwǔ firmly declined.
In the third month,
Shénwǔ wanted to marry his daughter to Líshēng's (蠡升) crown prince.
Waiting for them to be unprepared,
on the *xīnyǒu* day (辛酉),
he secretly led his army to attack them.
Their northern king cut off Líshēng's (蠡升) head and sent it.
His followers then enthroned his son, Nánhǎi Wáng (南海王).
Shénwǔ attacked them again
and captured Nánhǎi Wáng (南海王) and his younger brothers Xīhǎi Wáng (西海王) and Běihǎi Wáng (北海王), as well as the Empress, high officials, and others, totaling over four hundred people,
and fifty thousand households of Hú (胡) and Wèi (魏) people.
On the *rénshēn* day (壬申),
Shénwǔ held court at Yè (鄴).
In the fourth month,
Shénwǔ requested different provisions for the relocated people according to their status.
On the *jiǎyín* day (甲寅) of the ninth month,
Shénwǔ noted that many provincial, commandery, and county officials were acting unlawfully,
and requested to dispatch envoys to inquire about the people's suffering.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day (甲子) of the first month of the third year,
Shénwǔ led Kùdí Gān (厙狄干) and ten thousand cavalry to attack Xi Xī Wèi (西魏) Xiàzhōu (夏州).
He did not cook his food,
arriving in four days.
Binding spears together as ladders,
he entered the city at night,
captured its Cìshǐ (刺史) Fèi Yětóu Húbá Émítū (費也頭斛拔俄彌突),
〔一０〕and subsequently employed him.
He left Dūdū (都督) Zhāng Qióng (張瓊) to garrison it,
and relocated five thousand households of their tribes back.
The Western Wèi (西魏) Língzhōu Cìshǐ (靈州刺史) Cáo Ní (曹泥) and his son-in-law Liángzhōu Cìshǐ (涼州刺史) Liú Fēng (劉豐) sent envoys requesting to defect.
Zhōu Wén (周文) besieged Ní (泥),
flooding the city with water,
leaving four *chǐ* (尺) of it unsubmerged.
Shénwǔ ordered Āzhìluó (阿至羅) to dispatch thirty thousand cavalry to directly cross Língzhōu (靈州),
circling around to the rear of the Western army,
capturing fifty horses,
whereupon the Western army retreated.
Shénwǔ led cavalry to welcome Ní (泥) and Fēng (豐),
relocated five thousand of their remaining households back,
and restored Ní's (泥) official titles.
Wèi Dì issued an edict to bestow the Nine Marks of Distinction (九錫) upon Shénwǔ,
but he firmly declined, and it was halted.
In the second month,
Shénwǔ ordered Āzhìluó (阿至羅) to press the Western Wèi (西魏) Qínzhōu Cìshǐ (秦州刺史) Jiànzhōng Wáng Wànsì Pǔbō (建忠王万俟普撥),
and Shénwǔ supported him with his troops.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day (甲午) of the sixth month,

Pǔbō (普撥), along with his son Tàizǎi Shòuluògān (太宰受洛干), Bīnzhōu Cìshǐ (豳州刺史) Chìgān Bǎolè (叱干寶樂), Right Guard General Pòliùhán Cháng (破六韓常), and over three hundred commanders, surrendered with their tribes.
〔一一〕
On the *dīnghài* day (丁亥) of the eighth month,
Shénwǔ requested that measures and weights be standardized
and promulgated throughout the realm.
On the *xīnhài* day (辛亥) of the ninth month,
the Fénzhōu (汾州) Hú (胡) kings Tiáochù (迢觸) and Cáo Èrlóng (曹貳龍) gathered followers and rebelled,
appointing officials
and establishing the era name Píngdū (平都).
Shénwǔ attacked and pacified them.
On the *dīngchǒu* day (丁丑) of the twelfth month,
Shénwǔ marched west from Jìnyáng (晉陽),
sending concurrently Púyè Xíngtái (僕射行臺) Rǔyáng Wáng Xiān (汝陽王暹) and Sītú (司徒) Gāo Áng (高昂) to head for Shàngluò (上洛),
and Dàdūdū (大都督) Dòu Tài (竇泰) to enter through Tóngguān (潼關).
On the *guǐchǒu* day (癸丑) of the first month of the fourth year,
Dòu Tài's (竇泰) army was defeated, and he committed suicide.
Shénwǔ reached Pújīn (蒲津),
but as the ice was thin, he could not go to rescue them,
so he returned with his army.
Gāo Áng (高昂) attacked and captured Shàngluò (上洛).
On the *yǐyǒu* day (乙酉) of the second month,
Shénwǔ reported that the nine prefectures of Bìng (并), Sì (肆), Fén (汾), Jiàn (建), Jìn (晉), Dōngyōng (東雍), Nánfén (南汾), Tài (泰), and Shǎn (陝) suffered from frost and drought,
the people were starving and scattered,
and requested that granaries be opened in those areas for relief.
〔一二〕
On the *rénshēn* day (壬申) of the sixth month,
Shénwǔ went to Tiānchí (天池),
where he found an auspicious stone,
on which characters subtly rose, reading:
"Liù Wáng Sān Chuān" (六王三川).
In the eighth month of the fourth year, on the *Guǐsì* day,
Shénwǔ was about to lead a western expedition.
He gathered troops from Yè at Jìnyáng.
The Palace General Cáo Wèizǔ said:
"This is not advisable.
Now, in the eighth month, the west rules,
and with the energy of death countering the energy of life,
it will be disadvantageous for the guest,
though favorable for the host.
If the army proceeds,
the great general will be harmed."
Shénwǔ did not heed him.
Ever since the Eastern and Western Wèi forces clashed,
there had always been formations of yellow and black ants in Yè.
Diviners considered the yellow ones to be the color of the Eastern Wèi's military uniforms,
and the black ones to be the color of the Western Wèi's military uniforms.

was exhausted,
humanity and spirits were in despair,
a multitude of rebels surged to the heavens,
carving up the four seas.
The land and its subjects
were virtually no longer Wèi's.
Qí Xiànwǔ Wáng (齊獻武王) answered the call of the era and lent his hand,
soaring like a phoenix and leaping like a dragon.
Dì,
in response to the aspirations of all nations,
to eternally advance auspiciousness,
and protect and bless Qí,
thereby extending it to an endless reign.
On this day,
the capital obtained a red sparrow,
which was presented at the southern altar.
After the ceremony was complete,
he returned to the palace
and held court in the Tàijí Qiándiàn.
A decree stated:
“Being esteemed without possessing virtue,
replacing punishment with ritual,
being trusted without speaking,
and coming before spring and after autumn.
Thus it is known that the transformation of compassion
is a single principle for Heaven and humanity,
and the way of broad leniency
is the same in ancient and modern times.
I, being of shallow virtue,
have achieved no remarkable deeds.
Formerly, the late Xiànwǔ Wáng encountered a time when Wèi was in decline,
the nine tripods were departing;
he then marshalled the marquises and counts,
and issued a grand proclamation to Yān and Zhào,
rescuing those who had fallen,
and causing the lost to be preserved.
Wénxiāng Wáng outwardly displayed military prowess,
and inwardly possessed brilliant virtue.
He inherited the martial legacy of his predecessors,
expanding territory and subduing distant lands.
Over two decades passed,
and he presided over two capitals;
justice was served in legal cases,
and songs of praise were sung.
Therefore, the Wèi Emperor humbly followed the celestial mandate,
and, recalling the tradition of yielding the throne,
looked to Táng and Yú from afar,
ultimately renouncing his position as if shedding a sandal.
Indeed, my profound worries were unceasing,
my ambition was in Yángchéng;
but the sincerity and loyalty of all the ducal ministers became ever more urgent,
thus the succession was passed to me,
placing me above the people,
like wading through deep water,
with concerns throughout the day.
Upon first departing Jìnyáng,
a nine-tailed fox appeared as an auspicious omen.
At the outer altar, Heaven was invoked,
and a red sparrow demonstrated auspiciousness.
You, my civil and military officials of undivided loyalty,
my generals, my limbs and claws,
who assisted the late kings,
and were able to accomplish great deeds,
may your sincerity and integrity be eternally remembered,
and may you share in this auspiciousness.
I wish to share with the myriad people the beginning of this day;
let there be a great amnesty throughout the realm.
The eighth year of Wǔdìng is hereby changed to the first year of Tiānbǎo.
All officials shall be promoted in rank;
all adult males shall be granted titles of nobility;
widows, orphans, the six infirm, righteous husbands, and chaste wives shall each receive commendations and rewards according to their circumstances.”
On the day Jǐwèi,
a decree enfeoffed the Wèi Emperor as Zhōngshān Wáng,
with a fief of ten thousand households;
when submitting memorials, he was not to address himself as a subject;
responses to him were not to be called decrees;
he was to display the Son of Heaven's banners;
follow the Wèi calendar;
and ride in a vice-chariot of the five seasons.
The king's sons were enfeoffed as Xiàn Gōng,
with a thousand households each;
he was granted ten thousand bolts of silk,
ten million cash,
twenty thousand shí of grain,
two hundred servants,
one watermill,
one hundred qǐng of land,
and one garden.
A decree posthumously honored the Imperial Ancestor Wénmù Wáng as Wénmù Huángdì,
his consort as Wénmù Huánghòu,
the Imperial Father Xiànwǔ Wáng as Xiànwǔ Huángdì,
and the Imperial Brother Wénxiāng Wáng as Wénxiāng Huángdì.
The titles for the ancestors and progenitors
were to be discussed externally and swiftly reported.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
the Queen Dowager Wáng Tàihòu was honored as Huáng Tàihòu.
On the day Yǐchǒu,
a decree ordered the reduction of titles and ranks bestowed by the Wèi court, each according to its degree.
However, those from Xìndū who were righteous and loyal, and those who exerted themselves for the hegemonic court,
as well as those who came from the west, and those who came from the south and submitted since the sixth year of Wǔdìng,
were not subject to this reduction.
On the day Xīnwèi,
grand envoys were dispatched to the four directions,
to observe local customs,
inquire about the people's hardships,
strictly instruct local officials,
urge them to be honest and fair,
promote benefits and eliminate harms,
and strive to ensure peace and tranquility.
If any laws were inconvenient for the times,
or policies were incomplete in their execution,
they were to list the gains and losses in detail
and report back.
On the day Jiǎxū,
the ancestral tablets were moved to the Tàimiào.
On the day Jǐmǎo in the sixth month,
Gāolì sent envoys to pay tribute.
On the day Xīnsì,
a decree stated:
“Recently, customs have become degenerate,
and superficial competition daily increases.
When families have auspicious or inauspicious events,
they strive for extravagance and novelty.
The expenses of marriages and funerals,
the lavishness of carriages, clothes, food, and drink,
exhaust the annual income
to accumulate daily wealth.
Furthermore, male servants wear gold and jade,
and female servants wear damask and silk.
Initially, novelty was considered remarkable,
then surpassing what came before was deemed beautiful.
Upper and lower, noble and humble,
there is no longer any distinction.
Now that the destiny is to renew,
I wish to eradicate past evils,
return to simplicity and purity,
and guide the people's conduct.
Let regulations be established according to circumstances,
so that frugality may be achieved moderately.”
Another decree enfeoffed Chóngshèng Hóu with one hundred households,
to maintain the sacrifices to Kǒngzǐ,
and ordered Lǔ Jùn to timely repair the temple structures,
striving for the utmost reverence and commendation.
A decree ordered the dispatch of envoys to offer sacrifices at the Five Sacred Mountains and Four Great Rivers.
The shrines of Yáo and temples of Shùn,
down to Kǒng Fù, Lǎo Jūn, and others recorded in the sacrificial canon,
were all to be honored without omission.
A decree stated:
“The two commanderies of Bóhǎi and Chánglè in Jìzhōu
were the first enfeoffed states of the former Emperor,
and the places where the righteous banner was first raised.
Tàiyuán in Bìngzhōu and Qíjùn in Qīngzhōu
were where the hegemonic enterprise resided,
and the foundation of royal authority.
When a noble man acts,
he values not forgetting his origin.
I wish to extend this benevolence,
and exempt their land taxes.
Qíjùn and Bóhǎi shall both be exempted for one year,
Chánglè for two years,
and Tàiyuán for three years.”

A decree ordered that the late Tàifù Sūn Téng, late Tàibǎo Wèi Jǐng, late Dàsīmǎ Lóu Zhāo, late Sītú Gāo Áng, late Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè Mùróng Shàozōng, late Lǐngjūn Wànqí Gān, late Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ Duàn Róng, late Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi Liú Guì, late Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi Dòu Tài, late Yīnzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Fēng, late Jìzhōu Cìshǐ Cài Jùn, and others who assisted the former Emperor,
and supported the imperial foundation,
some of whom unfortunately died early,
or perished in royal service,
should have envoys dispatched to their tombs to offer sacrifices,
and to comfort and inquire after their wives and children,
extending solace to the living and the deceased.
Another decree enfeoffed the imperial kinsman Gāo Yuè as Qīnghé Wáng,
Gāo Lóngzhī as Píngyuán Wáng,
Gāo Guīyàn as Píngqín Wáng,
Gāo Sīzōng as Shàngluò Wáng,
Gāo Chángbì as Guǎngwǔ Wáng,
Gāo Pǔ as Wǔxīng Wáng,
Gāo Ziyuàn as Píngchāng Wáng,
Gāo Xiǎnguó as Xiānglè Wáng,
Gāo Ruì as Zhàojùn Wáng,
Gāo Xiàoxù as Xiūchéng Wáng.
Another decree enfeoffed the meritorious officials Kùdí Gān as Zhāngwǔ Wáng,
Húlǜ Jīn as Xiányáng Wáng,
Hébá Rén as Āndìng Wáng,
Hán Guǐ as Āndé Wáng,
Kězhūhún Dàoyuán as Fúfēng Wáng,
Péng Lè as Chénliú Wáng,
Pān Xiānglè as Hédōng Wáng.
On the day Guǐwèi,
a decree enfeoffed his younger brothers: Jùn, Cìshǐ of Qīngzhōu, as Yǒng'ān Wáng;
Yān, Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè, as Píngyáng Wáng;
Yóu, Cìshǐ of Dìngzhōu, as Péngchéng Wáng;
Yǎn, Yítóng Sānsī, as Chángshān Wáng;
Huàn, Cìshǐ of Jìzhōu, as Shàngdǎng Wáng;
Yù, Yítóng Sānsī, as Xiāngchéng Wáng;
Zhàn, Yítóng Sānsī, as Chángguǎng Wáng;
Jiē as Rènchéng Wáng;
Shí as Gāoyáng Wáng;
Jì as Bólíng Wáng;
Níng as Xīnpíng Wáng;
Rùn as Féngxǔ Wáng;
Qià as Hànyáng Wáng.
On the *dīnghài* day,
an edict was issued to enthrone Prince Yīn 殷 as Crown Prince,
and Queen Lǐ 李 to be Empress.
On the *gēngyín* day,
an edict appointed Grand Tutor Kùdí Gàn 厙狄干 as Grand Chancellor (Tàizǎi 太宰),
Minister of Works (Sītú 司徒) Péng Lè 彭樂 as Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi 太尉),
Minister of Education (Sīkōng 司空) Pān Xiānglè 潘相樂 as Minister of Works,
and *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī* 開府儀同三司 Sīmǎ Zǐrú 司馬子如 as Minister of Education.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
the former Grand Commandant and Prince of Qīnghé 清河, Yuè 岳, was appointed as *Shǐchíjié Píqi Dàjiāngjūn Sīzhōumù* 使持節、驃騎大將軍、司州牧.
On the *rénchén* day,
an edict stated:
"From now on,
all memorials and discussions on affairs of state, if they concern vital and confidential matters,
the appropriate officials shall submit them to Us."
On the *jǐhài* day,
to mark the Crown Prince's first entry into the Eastern Palace,
a general amnesty was declared for those sentenced to death or lesser crimes in the imperial domain and Bīngzhōu 並州;
for other prefectures, those sentenced to death were pardoned,
and all those sentenced to penal servitude or banishment or lesser penalties were fully pardoned.
In autumn, on the *xīnhài* day of the seventh month,
an edict honored Concubine Yuán 元, wife of Emperor Wénxiāng 文襄, as Empress Wénxiāng,
and her palace was named Jìngdé 靜德.
Another edict enfeoffed Xiàowǎn 孝琬, son of Emperor Wénxiāng, as Prince of Héjiān 河間,
and Xiàoyú 孝瑜 as Prince of Hénán 河南.
On the *yǐmǎo* day,
Shàngshū Lìng 尚書令 and Prince of Píngyuán 平原, Lóngzhī 隆之, was appointed to oversee the affairs of the Secretariat (Shàngshū Shì 尚書事);
Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè 尚書左僕射 and Prince of Píngyáng 平陽, Yān 淹, was appointed Shàngshū Lìng.
Another edict stated:
"The ancients wore deer-skin for clothes
and made tents from book-sacks.
They cherished abundant virtue,
and their elegant style is still imaginable.
The various rare and splendid silks in the Wei imperial treasury that are usually not given to people,
being merely accumulated,
should all be ordered to be taken out
and sent to the rear imperial garden
to be used for the seven-day banquet and bestowals."
In the eighth month,
an edict commanded commanderies and states to establish schools and academies,
widely recruit talented and outstanding individuals,
and promote Confucian customs.
The students of the Guózǐxiàng 國子學亦 should also be selected and appointed according to old regulations,
obediently following their teachers' instructions
and diligently studying the Rites Classics.
The fifty-two stone steles of Cài Yōng 蔡邕's classics, transported earlier by Emperor Wénxiāng,
should immediately be moved to the academic halls
and set up in order.
Another edict stated:
"Those who can speak frankly and offer righteous remonstrance,
without fearing punishment or blame,
forthright like Zhū Yún 朱雲,
and outspoken like Zhōu Shě 周舍,
who can enlighten Our mind
and refresh Our heart,
assisting Us, the sovereign,
and benefiting the common people,
shall certainly be favored with honor and emoluments,
and treated exceptionally."
It also stated:
"All officials who govern the people
should focus intently on agriculture and sericulture,
diligently encouraging and instructing,
to broadly harness the benefits of heaven and earth
to prepare for disasters of flood and drought."
On the *gēngyín* day,
an edict stated:
"Being of limited virtue,
We have succeeded to the great royal enterprise.
We contemplate how to praise great achievements
and broadcast them for ten thousand ages.
Although the court historians wield their brushes,
ensuring that what is heard is not lost,
We still fear that some scattered words of beauty might be overlooked
and occasionally not recorded.
All royal dukes and officials, civil and military, great and small,
down to the common people,
and even Buddhist monks and nuns,
whether they personally heard Our commands
or relayed them through others,
should record anything worthy of being included in historical records
and submit it in a compiled list."
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
an edict stated:
"The 'Línzhǐ Rules' 麟趾格, settled upon during the Wei dynasty,
became a universal system,
which government offices applied,
but it is still not entirely perfect.
The various officials should be ordered to further discuss and research it.
The methods for appropriate governance
should first fully address critical matters,
guiding the main principles and detailing the articles,
ensuring nothing is omitted."
In the ninth month, on the *guǐchǒu* day,

Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍, Chējì Jiāngjūn 車騎將軍, Leader of the Eastern Yi Colonel (Lǐng Dōngyí Xiàowèi 領東夷校尉), Duke of Kāiguó 開國 of Liáodōng Commandery 遼東郡, King of Gāolì 高麗, Chéng 成, was appointed as *Shǐchíjié Shìzhōng Píqi Dàjiāngjūn Lǐnghù Dōngyí Xiàowèi* 使持節、侍中、驃騎大將軍、領護東夷校尉,
with his titles of King and Duke remaining as before.

An edict recognized Liáng 梁 attendant minister (*Shìzhōng* 侍中), *Shǐchíjié* 使持節, *Jiǎhuángyuè* 假黃鉞, Grand General commanding all military affairs inside and outside (*Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūnshì Dàjiāngjūn* 都督中外諸軍事大將軍), acting with Imperial Authority (*Chéngzhì* 承制), Prince of Shàolíng 邵陵 Xiāo Lún 蕭綸, as King of Liáng.
On the *gēngwǔ* day,
the Emperor went to Jìnyáng 晉陽
to pay respects at the imperial mausoleum.
On this day, the Crown Prince entered and resided in the Liángfēng Táng 涼風堂 to supervise all state affairs.
In winter, on the *jǐmǎo* day of the tenth month,
the full imperial equipage was prepared,
the golden chariot was mounted,
and the Emperor entered Jìnyáng Palace
to pay respects to the Empress Dowager in the inner hall.
On the *xīnsì* day,
a partial amnesty was granted to prisoners in the four prisons of Jìnyáng County 晉陽縣, Tàiyuán Commandery 太原郡, Bīngzhōu, and the Grand Chancellor's Office.
On the *guǐwèi* day,
the Rúrú 茹茹 state sent envoys with tribute.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
Tèjìn 特進 Yuán Sháo 元韶 was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè,
and Bīngzhōu Governor Duàn Sháo 段韶 was appointed Shàngshū Yòupúyè 尚書右僕射.
On the *bǐngxū* day,
the Tǔyùhún 吐谷渾 state sent envoys with tribute.
On the *rénchén* day,
the Grand Chancellor's Office was abolished,
retaining the Cavalry Bureau (*Qíbīng Cáo* 騎兵曹) and Foreign Affairs Bureau (*Wàibīng Cáo* 外兵曹),
each establishing a separate department
to handle confidential matters independently.
In the eleventh month,
Emperor Wén of Zhōu 周 文帝 led his troops to Shǎnchéng 陝城,
divided his cavalry to cross north,
and reached Jiànzhōu 建州.
On the *jiǎyín* day,
Xiāo Yì 蕭繹, Prince of Xiāngdōng 湘東 of Liáng, sent envoys with tribute.
On the *bǐngyín* day,
the Emperor personally led the army and encamped east of the city.
Emperor Wén of Zhōu, hearing of the Emperor's imposing military presence,
sighed:
"Gāo Huān 高歡 is not dead!"
And then retreated his army.
On the *gēngwǔ* day,
the Emperor returned to the palace.
In the twelfth month, on the *dīngchǒu* day,
the Rúrú and Kùmòxī 庫莫奚 states both sent envoys with tribute.
On the *xīnchǒu* day,
the Emperor arrived from Jìnyáng.
In the second year, spring, on the *dīngwèi* day of the first month,
Xiāo Yì 蕭繹, Prince of Xiāngdōng of Liáng, sent envoys with tribute.
On the *xīnhài* day,
rites were performed at the Round Hill (Yuánqiū 圓丘),
with Emperor Shénwǔ 神武 as co-worshipper.
On the *guǐhài* day,
the Emperor personally plowed the sacred field (jítián 籍田) in the eastern suburbs.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
former Imperial Yellow Gate Attendant (Huángmén Shìláng 黃門侍郎) Yuán Shìbǎo 元世寶 and Palace Attendant (Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng 通直散騎侍郎) Péng Guìpíng 彭貴平 conspired to rebel;
they were spared death but exiled to the border.
Rites were performed at the Grand Ancestral Temple.
On the *jiǎxū* day,
the Emperor boated east of the city.
In the second month, on the *rénchén* day,
Grand Commandant Péng Lè conspired to rebel
and was executed.
On the *rén'yín* day,
the Rúrú state sent envoys with tribute.
In the third month, on the *bǐngwǔ* day,
Yù 淯, Prince of Xiāngchéng 襄城, died.
On the *jǐwèi* day,
an edict recognized Xiāo Yì, Prince of Xiāngdōng of Liáng, acting with Imperial Authority, as *Liáng Shǐchíjié Jiǎhuángyuè Xiàngguó* 梁使持節、假黃鉞、相國,
established the Liáng Platform (Liángtái 梁臺),
to oversee all state affairs,
and act with Imperial Authority.

Li Jǐngshèng 李景盛, Governor of Jiāozhōu 交州; Mǎ Sōngrén 馬嵩仁, Governor of Liángzhōu 梁州; Xiàhóu Zhēnqià 夏侯珍洽, Governor of Yìzhōu 義州; Lǐ Hàn 李漢, Governor of Xīnzhōu 新州, and others, all led their prefectures to submit.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
Minister of Education Sīmǎ Zǐrú was dismissed for misconduct.
In summer, on the *rénchén* day of the fourth month,
King of Liáng Xiāo Yì sent envoys with tribute.
In the intercalary month, on the *yǐchǒu* day,
the Shìwěi 室韋 state sent envoys with tribute.
In the fifth month, on the *bǐngxū* day,
Húxī Xiǎn 斛斯顯, Governor of Hézhōu 合州, attacked and captured Liáng's Lìyáng 歷陽 garrison.
On the *dīnghài* day,
the Gāolì state sent envoys with tribute.
In this month,
Hóu Jǐng 侯景 deposed Emperor Jiǎnwén 簡文 of Liáng
and enthroned Xiāo Dòng 蕭棟 as ruler.
In the sixth month, on the *gēngwǔ* day,
the former Minister of Education Sīmǎ Zǐrú was appointed Grand Commandant.
In the seventh month, on the *rénshēn* day,
Rúrú sent envoys with tribute.
On the *guǐyǒu* day,
Xíng Jǐngyuǎn 邢景遠, a Secretariat official (*Xíngtái Láng* 行臺郎), defeated Liáng's Lóng'ān 龍安 garrison
and captured its town defender Lǐ Luòwén 李洛文.
On the *jǐmǎo* day,
the Xiǎnyáng Palace 顯陽殿 was renamed Zhāoyáng Palace 昭陽殿.
In the ninth month, on the *rénshēn* day,
an edict exempted all entertainers, laborers, herdsmen, and various miscellaneous service personnel from their servitude, making them commoners (*báihù* 白戶).
On the *guǐsì* day,
the Emperor went to Zhào 趙 and Dìng 定 prefectures,
and then to Jìnyáng.
In winter, on the *wùshēn* day of the tenth month,
the Xuānguāng 宣光, Jiànshǐ 建始, Jiāfú 嘉福, and Rénshòu 仁壽 palaces were constructed.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
Xiāo Yì sent envoys with tribute.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
the spirit tablet of Emperor Wénxiāng was placed in the ancestral temple.
In the eleventh month,
Hóu Jǐng deposed the lord of Liáng,
and usurped the spurious imperial throne at Jiànyè,
proclaiming himself Hán.
In the twelfth month,
Zhōngshān Wáng passed away.
In the third year, spring, first month, on the day Bǐngshēn,
the Emperor personally campaigned against the Kùmòxī in Dài Jùn,
and severely defeated them,
capturing over a hundred thousand head of livestock,
which were distributed among the generals and soldiers with varying shares.
The Xī households were sent to Shāndōng to become commoners.
In the second month,
Rúrú lord Ānàguī was defeated by the Türks (lǔ),
and Guī committed suicide;
his crown prince Ānluóchén, and Guī's cousin Dēngzhù Sīlìfā, and Dēngzhù's son Kùtí, all led their multitudes and came to surrender.
The remaining Rúrú established Dēngzhù's second son Tiěfá as their lord.
On the day Xīnchǒu,
the Qìdān sent envoys to pay tribute.
In the third month, on the day Wùzǐ,
Sīzhōu Mù, Qīnghé Wáng Yuè, was appointed as Shǐchíjié, Nándào Dàdūdū;
Sītú Pān Xiànglè as Shǐchíjié, Dōngnán Dào Dàdūdū;
and Xíngtái Xīn Shù was ordered to lead troops for a southern campaign.
On the day Guǐsì,
an imperial edict promoted Liáng Wáng Xiāo Yì to be the lord of Liáng.
In summer, fourth month, on the day Rénshēn,
Dōngnán Dào Xíngtái Xīn Shù sent the Heirloom Seal of the Realm from Guǎnglíng.
On the day Jiǎshēn,
Lìbù Shàngshū Yáng Yīn was appointed Shàngshū Yòupúshè.
On the day Bǐngshēn,
the state of Shìwěi sent envoys to pay tribute.
In the sixth month, on the day Yǐhài,
Qīnghé Wáng Yuè and others returned with their troops.
On the day Dīngwèi,
the Emperor arrived from Jìnyáng.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
the Emperor went to Jìnyáng.
In the ninth month, on the day Xīnmǎo,
the Emperor traveled from Bìngzhōu to Líshí.
In winter, tenth month, on the day Yǐwèi,
he reached Huánglúlǐng,
and then began constructing the Great Wall,
extending north to Shègānshù, over four hundred *lǐ*,
establishing thirty-six garrisons.
In the eleventh month, on the day Xīnsì,
Liáng Wáng Xiāo Yì ascended the imperial throne in Jiānglíng,
known as Yuán Dì,
and sent envoys to pay tribute.
In the twelfth month, on the day Rénzǐ,
the Emperor returned to the palace.
On the day Wùwǔ,
the Emperor went to Jìnyáng.
In the fourth year, spring, first month, on the day Bǐngzǐ,
the Shānhú besieged Líshí.
On the day Wùyín,
the Emperor campaigned against them,
but before he arrived,
the Hú had already fled,
so he proceeded to inspect the Sānduī garrisons,
and returned after a grand hunt.
On the day Wùyín,
the Kùmòxī sent envoys to pay tribute.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
new coins were recast,
with the inscription
“Chángpíng Wǔzhū.”
In the second month,
Dēngzhù, father of Rúrú lord Tiěfá, and his son Kùtí, were sent back north.
Tiěfá was soon killed by the Qìdān,
and the people of the state re-established Dēngzhù as their lord,
but he was again killed by his grandee Āfùtí and others,
and the people of the state re-established Kùtí as their lord.
In summer, fourth month, on the day Wùxū,
the Emperor returned to the palace.
On the day Wùwǔ,
there was a great sound like thunder in the southwest.
In the fifth month, on the day Gēngwǔ,
the Emperor held a military hunt at Línlǜ Shān.
On the day Wùzǐ,
he returned to the palace.
In the ninth month,
the Qìdān violated the frontier.
On the day Rénwǔ,
the Emperor made a northern inspection of Jì, Dìng, Yōu, and Ān (prefectures),
and then campaigned north against the Qìdān.
In winter, tenth month, on the day Dīngyǒu,
the Emperor reached Píngzhōu,
and then proceeded from the western route to Qùchángqiàn.
An edict ordered Sītú Pān Xiànglè to lead five thousand elite cavalry from the eastern route to Qīngshān.
On the day Xīnchǒu,
they reached Báiláng Chéng.
On the day Rényín,
they passed through Chānglí Chéng.
Another edict ordered Āndé Wáng Hán Guǐ to lead four thousand elite cavalry eastward,
to cut off the Qìdān's escape route.
On the day Guǐmǎo,
they reached Yángshī Shuǐ,
traveling double the normal distance day and night,
to surprise and attack the Qìdān.
On the day Jiǎchén,
the Emperor personally crossed mountains and ridges,
leading his soldiers,
directing and inspiring the assault,
severely defeating them,
capturing over a hundred thousand people and hundreds of thousands of head of livestock.
Pān Xiànglè also severely defeated another Qìdān detachment at Qīngshān.
All the captured people were distributed among various prefectures.
During this campaign,
the Emperor went bareheaded and bared his shoulders,
traveling day and night without rest,
covering over a thousand *lǐ*,
subsisting only on meat and water,
his martial spirit ever more fierce.
On the day Dīngwèi,
he reached Yíngzhōu.
On the day Dīngsì,
he ascended Jiéshí Shān,
overlooking the vast sea.
In the eleventh month, on the day Jǐwèi,
the Emperor traveled from Píngzhōu,
and then went to Jìnyáng.
In the intercalary month, on the day Rényín,
the Liáng Emperor sent envoys to seek an alliance.
In the twelfth month, on the day Jǐwèi,
the Türks again attacked the Rúrú,
and the Rúrú nation fled south.
On the day Guǐhài,
the Emperor campaigned north from Jìnyáng against the Türks,
and welcomed the Rúrú.
He then deposed their lord Kùtí,
and established Ānàguī's son Ānluóchén as their lord,
settling him in Mǎyì Chuān,
and providing him with provisions, food, silk, and cloth.
He personally pursued the Türks in Shuòzhōu;
the Türks requested to surrender,
which was granted, and he returned.
Thereupon, tributes followed continuously.
In the fifth year, spring, first month, on the day Guǐsì,
the Emperor campaigned against the Shānhú,
taking the Líshí route.
He sent Tàishī, Xiányáng Wáng Húlǜ Jīn, via the Xiǎnzhōu route,
and Chángshān Wáng Yǎn via the Jìnzhōu route,
to attack them from different directions,
severely defeating them,
beheading tens of thousands,
and capturing over a hundred thousand head of livestock,
thereby pacifying Shílóu.
Shílóu was extremely precipitous,
a place unreachable since the time of Wèi.
Consequently, the Shānhú, near and far, were all overawed and submitted.
This month, Zhōu Wén Dì deposed the Western Wèi lord,
and established Qí Wáng Kuò,
who became Gōng Dì.
In the third month,
the Rúrú Ānluóchén rebelled.
The Emperor personally campaigned against him,
and severely defeated him,
and Ānluóchén and his son fled north.
Tàibǎo Hèbá Rén was dismissed for violating orders.
In summer, fourth month,
the Rúrú raided Sìzhōu.
On the day Dīngsì,
the Emperor campaigned against them from Jìnyáng,
and upon reaching Huángguā Duī in the prefecture,
the barbarian cavalry fled.
At that time, the main army had already returned,
but the Emperor led over a thousand cavalry under his command,
and encountered several tens of thousands of another Rúrú detachment,
who surrounded and pressed in from all sides.
The Emperor remained composed,
directing the tactical situation,
and the barbarian multitude wavered,
whereupon he unleashed his troops, broke through the encirclement, and escaped.
The barbarians then retreated,
and were pursued and attacked,
leaving dead bodies for twenty *lǐ*,
and Ānluóchén's wife and children, and over thirty thousand captives, were seized.
In the fifth month, on the day Dīnghài,
the states of Dìdòugān, Qìdān, and others, all sent envoys to pay tribute.
On the day Dīngwèi,
he campaigned north against the Rúrú,
and severely defeated them.
In the sixth month,
the Rúrú led their forces eastward,
intending to invade south.
The Emperor led light cavalry to intercept them at the foot of Jīnshān,
and the Rúrú, hearing of this, fled far away.
In autumn, seventh month, on the day Wùzǐ,
Sùshèn sent envoys to pay tribute.
On the day Rénchén,
pardons were granted to criminals.
On the day Gēngxū,
the Emperor arrived back from the northern campaign.
In the eighth month, on the *dìngsì* day,
the Türks sent envoys to present tribute at court.
On the *gēngzǐ* day,
Yuè, Prince of Qīnghé and Governor of Sīzhōu, was appointed Grand Tutor (Tàibǎo);
Wèi Càn, Minister of Works (Sīkōng), was appointed Minister over the Masses (Sītú);
〔一○〕Hóumòchén Xiāng, Grand Preceptor to the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Tàishī), was appointed Minister of Works (Sīkōng);
Yān, Prince of Píngyáng and President of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng), was made Supervisor of the Department of State Affairs (Lù Shàngshū Shì);
Yǎn, Prince of Chángshān, was appointed President of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng);
Huàn, Prince of Shàngdǎng and Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng), was appointed Left Assistant of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè).
On the *yǐhài* day,
Yuán Xù, with the title of Yítóng Sānsī, was granted death for his crimes.
On the *dīngchǒu* day,
the Emperor visited Jìnyáng.
On the *jǐmǎo* day,
Gāo Lóngzhī, Prince of Píngyuán, with the titles of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī and Supervisor of the Department of State Affairs (Lù Shàngshū Shì), passed away.
In this month,

an imperial edict commanded Yǎn, Prince of Chángshān, Huàn, Prince of Shàngdǎng, Yuè, Prince of Qīnghé, Duàn Sháo, Prince of Píngyuán, and others, to lead their troops to build Fá'è City, Xīn City, Yán City, and Hénán City southwest of Luòyáng.
In the ninth month,
the Emperor personally visited the sites,
intending to lure the Zhōu army out.
As the Zhōu army did not emerge,
he then returned to Jìnyáng.
In winter, the tenth month,
Western Wèi attacked Liáng Yuándì at Jiānglíng.
An imperial edict ordered Yuè, Prince of Qīnghé, Pān Xiānglè, Prince of Hédōng, Duàn Sháo, Prince of Píngyuán, and others, to lead their troops to rescue him.
Before they arrived, Jiānglíng fell,
and Liáng Yuándì was killed by Yú Jǐn, a general of Western Wèi.
Liáng general Wáng Sēngbiàn, then in Jiànkāng,
together with others, enthroned Xiāo Fāngzhì, Prince of Jìn'ān, as Grand Preceptor (Tàizǎi) and General-in-chief of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital (Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhūjūn),
and allowed him to establish all officials by imperial decree.
In the twelfth month, on the *gēngshēn* day,
the Emperor toured north to Dáshù Lǐng,
surveyed the treacherous terrain of the mountains and rivers,
and intended to build the Great Wall.
In the sixth year, spring, the first month, on the *rén'yín* day,
Yuè, Prince of Qīnghé, led a multitude of troops across the river,
and captured Xiàshǒu.
He sent Lù Fǎhé, Inspector of Yǐngzhōu of Liáng.
〔一一〕An imperial edict appointed Xiāo Míng, Gentleman-in-Waiting (Sànqí Chángshì) and Marquis of Zhēnyáng of Liáng, as the ruler of Liáng,
and dispatched Huàn, Prince of Shàngdǎng and Left Assistant of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè), to lead troops to escort him.
In the second month, on the *jiǎzǐ* day,

Lù Fǎhé was appointed as Envoy with Imperial Credentials (Shǐ Chíjíe), Military Governor (Dūdū) of all Military Affairs in the ten prefectures of Jīng, Yōng, Jiāng, Bā, Liáng, Yì, Xiāng, Wàn, Jiāo, and Guǎng,〔一二〕Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi Gōng), Grand Commander (Dà Dūdū), and Grand Administrator of the Southwestern Circuit (Xīnán Dào Dà Xíngtái).

Sòng Zhǐ, General Who Guards the North (Zhèn Běi Jiāngjūn), Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), and Inspector of Jīngzhōu of Liáng, was appointed as Envoy with Imperial Credentials (Shǐ Chíjíe), General of Agile Cavalry (Piāoqí Dà Jiāngjūn), and Inspector of Yǐngzhōu.
On the *jiǎxū* day,
Huàn, Prince of Shàngdǎng, captured Qiáojùn.
In the third month, on the *bǐngxū* day,
Huàn, Prince of Shàngdǎng, reached Dōngguān,
beheaded the Liáng general Péi Zhīhéng,
and captured or beheaded several thousand men.
On the *bǐngshēn* day,
the Emperor arrived from Jìnyáng.
He enfeoffed Shìzōng’s two sons, Xiào Háng as Prince of Guǎngníng,
and Yánzōng as Prince of Āndé.
On the *wùxū* day,
the Emperor attended to lawsuits and pronounced judgments in Zhaóyáng Hall.
In summer, the fourth month, on the *gēngshēn* day,
the Emperor went to Jìnyáng.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
Xiāo Guǐ, with the title of Yítóng, captured Jìnxī City of Liáng,
and made it into Jiāngzhōu.
On the *wùyín* day,
the Türks sent envoys to present tribute at court.
Lǐ Shānhuā, a rebel from Liáng, proclaimed himself Son of Heaven,
and pressed upon Lúshān City.
In the fifth month, on the *yǐyǒu* day,
Lǐ Zhòngkǎn, the city defender, attacked and beheaded him.
On the *gēngyín* day,
the Emperor arrived from Jìnyáng.
Xiāo Míng entered Jiànyè.
On the *dīngwèi* day,
the Rúrú sent envoys to present tribute at court.
In the sixth month, on the *rénzǐ* day,
an imperial edict stated:
“The state of Liáng has met with calamity,
its ruler lost, its ministers dispersed;
far in that fiery region,
it is completely overgrown with thorns.
To restore what has fallen and maintain the broken line,
is our righteous duty.
By installing a senior ruler
and rescuing them from their perilous plight,
the ruler of Liáng, whom we escorted,
has already entered Jīnlíng.
Now that the tributary rituals have been performed,
the relationship of loyalty and righteousness should be firm.
The bird of Yuè, in its longing,
does not forget the southern branch.
Therefore, all Liáng people
should be permitted to return to their country,
and be dispatched with due ceremony.”
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
the Emperor went to Jìnyáng.
On the *rénshēn* day,
he personally launched a punitive expedition against the Rúrú.
On the *jiǎxū* day,
all armies assembled at Qílián Chǐ.
On the *yǐhài* day,
they exited the frontier pass,
and reached Kùdí Gǔ.
Within a hundred *lǐ* there was no water spring,
and the six armies suffered from thirst.
Shortly after, there was a heavy rain.
On the *wùyín* day,

Xiāo Míng, the ruler of Liáng, sent his son Zhāng, together with Yuán Bì, who held the concurrent post of Palace Attendant (Jiān Shìzhōng), and Yáng Yù, who held the concurrent post of Gentleman-in-Waiting (Jiān Sànqí Chángshì), to present a memorial as tribute.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the *jǐmǎo* day,
the Emperor stopped at Báidào,
left the baggage train,
and personally led five thousand light cavalry to pursue the Rúrú.
On the *rénwǔ* day,
they caught up with them at Huáishuò Town.
The Emperor personally braved arrows and stones,
repeatedly inflicting great defeats,
and reaching Wòyě.
He captured their Sīlì Āi'yān Lìlóu Ādì and Tùtóufà Yùjiǔlǘ Zhuàngyán,
as well as over twenty thousand people,
and hundreds of thousands of cattle and sheep.
The Rúrú Sīlì Yùjiǔlǘ Lǐ Jiātí, with several hundred of his troops, surrendered.
On the *rénchén* day,
the Emperor returned to Jìnyáng.
In the ninth month, on the *yǐmǎo* day,
the Emperor arrived from Jìnyáng.
In winter, the tenth month,
Liáng general Chén Bàxiān attacked Wáng Sēngbiàn,
killed him,
deposed Xiāo Míng,
and re-established Xiāo Fāngzhì as ruler.
On the *xīnhài* day,
the Emperor went to Jìnyáng.
In the eleventh month, on the *bǐngxū* day,
Gāolì sent envoys to present tribute at court.
Xú Sìhuī, Inspector of Qínzhōu of Liáng, Rèn Yuē, Inspector of Nányùzhōu, and others, attacked and occupied Shítóu City,
and brought their prefectures into allegiance.
On the *rénchén* day,
Grand Commander Xiāo Guǐ led his troops to the river,
and dispatched Commander Liǔ Dámó and others to cross the river and garrison Shítóu.
Zhào Yànshēn, Administrator of the Southeastern Circuit (Dōngnán Dào Xíngtái), captured five cities including Qínjùn,
with over twenty thousand households,
and pacified the local populace.
On the *jǐhài* day,
Yuè, Prince of Qīnghé, Grand Tutor (Tàibǎo) and Governor of Sīzhōu, passed away.
In this month,
Liǔ Dámó was attacked and pressed by Bàxiān,
and surrendered Shítóu.
In the twelfth month, on the *wùshēn* day,
the Kùmòxī sent envoys to present tribute at court.
In this year,
one million eight hundred thousand men were conscripted to build the Great Wall,
from Xiàkǒu north of Yōuzhōu to the capital, over nine hundred *lǐ*.
In the seventh year, spring, the first month, on the *jiǎchén* day,
the Emperor arrived from Jìnyáng.
He held a mounted archery contest west of Yèchéng,
and gathered a large crowd to watch it.
In the second month, on the *xīnwèi* day,
an imperial edict commanded Yǎn, Prince of Chángshān, and others, to read memorials and petitions in the Liángfēng Táng,
discuss and determine their merits and demerits,
and the Emperor personally made the final decisions.
In the third month, on the *dīngyǒu* day,
Grand Commander Xiāo Guǐ and others led their troops across the Jiāng River.
In summer, the fourth month, on the *yǐchǒu* day,
Lóu Ruì, with the title of Yítóng, led troops to suppress the Lúyáng Mán,
and greatly defeated them.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
〔一三〕an imperial edict commanded the construction of Jīnhuá Palace.
In the fifth month, on the *bǐngshēn* day,
Qià, Prince of Hànyáng, passed away.
In this month,
the Emperor decided to abstain from meat out of compassion,
and never ate it again.
In the sixth month, on the *yǐmǎo* day,
Xiāo Guǐ and others fought with the Liáng army west of Zhōngshān.
Encountering continuous rain,
they suffered a defeat.
Guǐ, and commanders Lǐ Xīguāng, Wáng Jìngbǎo, Dōngfāng Lǎo, and military aide Péi Yīngqǐ, were all lost.
Only two or three tenths of the soldiers scattered and returned.
On the *yǐchǒu* day,
Wáng Lín, Inspector of Xiāngzhōu of Liáng, presented a tamed elephant.
In this year,
the palaces of the Three Platforms were renovated and expanded.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the *jǐhài* day,
a general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire.
In the eighth month, on the *gēngshēn* day,
the Emperor went to Jìnyáng.
In the ninth month, on the *jiǎchén* day,
the Kùmòxī sent envoys to present tribute at court.
In winter, the tenth month, on the *bǐngxū* day,
the Khitan sent envoys to present tribute at court.
In this month,
two thousand six hundred widows from Shāndōng were conscripted to be given to soldiers;
one fifth of those with husbands were unjustly seized.
In this month,
Zhōu Wéndì passed away.
〔一四〕
In the eleventh month, on the day Rénzǐ,
an edict stated: "Kūnshān serves as the central peak,
hence the name Shénzhōu;
the boundless ocean acts as a pond,
thus it is called Chìxiàn.
When the common people prosper,
the herdsmen exist.
The systems of kings
have
evolved and changed successively.
When territorial divisions led to disaster,
they were first divided into twelve,
and once the lands and waters were pacified,
they reverted to nine Zhōus.
While the Dao may be complex or simple,
its essence lies in adapting to the times.
The Yīn dynasty followed the Xià dynasty,
making no fundamental changes.
Yet, the sun and moon revolve through their celestial positions,
and kings and dukes establish states in the earthly realm,
all to align with the profound cosmic order above
and correspond with the rivers and mountains below.
Reaching the Qín
administration,
which scourged the entire realm,
abolished feudal lords and appointed commandery governors,
treating the empire as its private domain.
When the two Hàn dynasties inherited this foundation,
and the Cáo and Mǎ families continued the legacy,
the gains and losses during that period
are too numerous to recount.
Since the late Xiàochāng reign of the Wèi dynasty,
it has repeatedly faced decline and adversity.
Emoluments were removed from the imperial house,
governance came from many factions,
officials lost their integrity,
and the common people suffered greatly.
Followers of the Bronze Horse and Iron Shin
factions,
companions of Black Mountain
and Green Colt,
rose violently in Jìn and Zhào,
and rampaged through Yān and Qín.
From then on, the social order collapsed,
and the established norms became chaotic.
This led to powerful
families and great clans
gathering and leading local communities,
ostensibly to serve the emperor,
but secretly appointing themselves.
Or, imperial princesses from external families,
whose female attendants exerted influence internally,
unscrupulously accepted bribes,
and initiated the establishment of Zhōu
and Jùn.
Dividing large units and combining small ones,
originally followed temporal expediency.
Dividing bamboo tallies and distributing symbols of authority
was done out of necessity.
The number of shepherds, governors, magistrates, and chiefs
was excessively increased,
seeking merit and recording achievements;
this truly
became a burden,
harming both public and private interests,
and its evils have long persisted.
It violated the principles of governance
and only incurred the cost of driving sheep.
Since then, these practices have continued,
without time for reform.
I, having reverently received the precious mandate
and respectfully presided over the eight directions,
in establishing states and managing the land,
strive for simplicity and ease.
I intend to calm the restless and restore tranquility,
to revert from extravagance to simplicity.
If there is a deviation from the
mean,
it should be rectified.
Observing past histories,
and listening to ancient sayings,
the Zhōu dynasty had Chéng and Kāng,
and the Hàn dynasty had Wén and Jǐng,
when the number of registered households was
the highest in ancient and modern times.
Yet,
the population is less than in former days,
while the number of governors and magistrates is double that of olden times.
This is not how to manage customs and regulate traditions,
or to provide guidance to the people.
Moreover, the Wǔlǐng mountains have submitted,
and the Sānjiāng rivers have been pacified,
expanding territory and opening borders,
with benefits reaching the Nánhǎi.
However, in remote and desolate areas,
there was formerly much pretense and falsity.
A town of a hundred households
would arbitrarily be given the name of a Zhōu,
and a population of three households
would be granted the empty title of a Jùn.
This is like a wooden dog,
or a mud dragon,
where seeking reality from the name
results in nothing.
Therefore, the present consolidations and abolitions
shall all follow a separate decree."
Thereupon, three Zhōu, one hundred fifty-three Jùn, five hundred eighty-nine Xiàn, two Zhèn, and twenty-six Shù were consolidated and abolished.
It was also decreed that Cìshǐ must all perform concurrent duties
and would not be provided with additional personnel.
[一五]
In the twelfth month,
Yǔwén Jué, chancellor of Western Wèi, received the Wèi abdication.
Previously,
from Xīhé Zǒngqín Shù eastward to the sea, a Great Wall had been built,
totaling over three thousand lǐ from east to west in successive constructions.
On average, there was one garrison every ten lǐ,
and key strategic points were established as Zhōu-Zhèn,
totaling twenty-five locations.
In the eighth year, in spring, the third month,
there was great heat,
and some people died from sunstroke.
In summer, the fourth month, on the day Gēngwǔ,
an edict prohibited the capture of shrimp, crabs, clams, and similar creatures,
permitting only fishing.
On the day Yǐyǒu,
an edict also completely banned private and public ownership of eagles and hawks.
Húli Jīn, Grand Preceptor and Prince of Xiányáng, was appointed Right Chancellor;
Kězhūhún Dàoyuán, former Grand General and Prince of Fúfēng, was appointed Grand Tutor;
Hèbá Rén, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, was appointed Grand Guardian;
Yǎn, Shàngshū Lìng and Prince of Chángshān, was appointed Sīkōng;
Zhàn, Lù Shàngshū Shì and Prince of Chángguǎng, was appointed Shàngshū Lìng;
Yáng Yīn, Shàngshū Yòu Púyè, was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè;
Cuī Xiān, who had been consolidated from Shàngshū Yòu Púyè, was appointed Shàngshū Yòu Púyè;
Huàn, Prince of Shàngdǎng, was appointed Lù Shàngshū Shì.
In this month,
the emperor practiced archery on horseback east of the capital.
An order was issued for all women in the capital to attend and watch,
with those who did not attend being punished by military law.
This continued for seven days.
In the fifth month, on the day Xīnyǒu,
Liú Xiàng, a commoner from Jìzhōu, conspired rebellion in the capital,
and his accomplices were all executed.
In autumn, the eighth month, on the day Jǐsì,
the Kùmò Xī sent envoys to pay tribute.
On the day Gēngchén,
an edict stated that for the Qiū, Jiāo, Dì, Xiá, and seasonal sacrifices,
all offerings should be purchased from the market.
The Shàoláo sacrifice must not involve dismemberment.
Officials concerned must supervise
to ensure abundant provisions.
For Nóngshè and Xiāncán,
only wine and meat are sufficient.
For Yú, Méi, wind, rain, Sīmín, Sīlù, Língxīng, and miscellaneous sacrifices,
fruits, cakes, wine, and dried meat are sufficient.
Only utmost sincerity and reverence should be exercised,
with the spirit of the deities being present.
From summer to the ninth month,
there was a great locust plague in six Zhōu north of the Yellow River, twelve Zhōu south of the Yellow River, and eight Jùn within the imperial domain.
In this month,
they flew to the capital,
obscuring the sun,
with a sound like wind and rain.
On the day Jiǎchén,
an edict exempted areas affected by the locusts from taxes for the current year.
In this month,
Yǔwén Hù, chief minister of Zhōu, killed his lord Emperor Mǐn and enthroned the emperor's younger brother Yù,
[一六] who became Emperor Míng.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day Yǐhài,
Chén Bàxiān assassinated his lord Fāng Zhì and enthroned himself,
becoming Emperor Wǔ of Chén.
He sent envoys to declare vassalage and pay tribute.
In this year,
a double wall was built within the Great Wall,
from Kùluòbá eastward to Wǔgē Shù,
totaling over four hundred lǐ.
In the ninth year, in spring, the second month, on the day Dīnghài,
criminals were pardoned.
On the day Jǐchǒu,
an edict limited burning the fields to the month of Zhòngdōng,
prohibiting the use of fire at other times,
to avoid harming insects and plants.
In the third month, on the day Dīngyǒu,
the emperor returned from Jìnyáng.
In summer, the fourth month, on the day Xīnsì,
a general amnesty was granted.
This summer,
there was a great drought.
Because prayers for rain were unanswered, the emperor
destroyed the temple of Xīmén Bào and
excavated his tomb.
There was a great locust plague east of the mountains,
and conscripted laborers were dispatched to catch and bury them in pits.
In this month,
Sīmǎ Xiāonàn, the Cìshǐ of Běiyùzhōu, rebelled with his city
and defected to Zhōu.
In the tenth year, tenth month,
Wénxuān passed away.
On the guǐmǎo day,
the Crown Prince ascended the imperial throne at the Xuāndé Hall in Jìnyáng,
proclaimed a general amnesty,
and universally promoted all civil and military officials, both inside and outside the court.
Those who had lost their official posts or noble ranks
were permitted to reclaim their former status.
On the gēngxū day,
the Empress Dowager was honored as Grand Empress Dowager,
and the Empress as Empress Dowager.
An imperial edict ordered that all soldiers in the nine provinces aged seventy and above be granted an official position,
and all military officers aged sixty and above, as well as those suffering from chronic illness and unable to serve,
were all discharged.
All construction works involving earth and timber, and all miscellaneous works using gold, copper, and iron,
were completely halted.
In the eleventh month, on the yǐmǎo day,
Húliù Jīn, Right Chancellor and King of Xiányáng, was appointed Left Chancellor.
Yǎn, Overseer of the Affairs of the Department of State Affairs and King of Chángshān, was appointed Grand Tutor.
Zhàn, Minister of Works and King of Chángguǎng, was appointed Grand Commandant.
Duàn Sháo, Minister of Works, was appointed Minister of Works (Sītú).
Yān, King of Píngyáng, was appointed Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
Shí, King of Gāoyáng, was appointed Left Grand Secretary of the Department of State Affairs.
Xiàowǎn, King of Héjiān, was appointed Governor of Sīzhōu.
Yàn Zǐxiàn, Imperial Attendant, was appointed Right Grand Secretary.
On the wùwǔ day,
envoys were dispatched to tour the four directions,
to inquire into the successes and failures of governance,
to observe the local customs,
and to ask about the people's hardships.
In the twelfth month, on the wùxū day,
Shàorén, King of Shàngdǎng, was re-enfeoffed as King of Yúyáng.
Shàoyì, King of Guǎngyáng, was re-enfeoffed as King of Fányáng.
Shàolián, King of Chánglè, was re-enfeoffed as King of Lǒngxī.
This year
was the first year of Wǔchéng of the Zhōu dynasty.
In the first year of Qiánmíng, gēngchén year,
spring, first month, on the guǐchǒu new moon day,
the reign title was changed.
On the jǐwèi day,
an edict was issued to lighten the corvée and taxes.
On the guǐhài day,
Shí, King of Gāoyáng, passed away.
In this month,
the imperial carriage arrived from Jìnyáng.
In the second month, on the jǐhài day,
Yǎn, Grand Tutor and King of Chángshān, was appointed Grand Preceptor and Overseer of the Affairs of the Department of State Affairs.
Zhàn, Grand Commandant and King of Chángguǎng, was appointed Grand Marshal and concurrently Overseer of the Affairs of the Department of State Affairs.
Guīyàn, Left Grand Secretary of the Department of State Affairs and King of Píngqín, was appointed Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
Ruì, King of Zhàojùn, was appointed Left Grand Secretary of the Department of State Affairs.
An edict released
all female relatives of former officials who had been confiscated into the palace or bestowed upon others.
On the jiǎchén day,
the Emperor visited Fānglínyuán Park,
personally reviewed the prisoners,
and those sentenced to death or lesser punishments were pardoned or had their sentences reduced, each according to their circumstances.
On the yǐsì day,
Yǎn, Grand Preceptor and King of Chángshān, fabricated an edict to execute Yáng Yīn, Minister of State Affairs; Yàn Zǐxiàn, Right Grand Secretary of the Department of State Affairs;
Kězhūhún Tiānhé, General of the Palace Guard; Sòng Qīndào, Imperial Attendant; and Zhèng Zǐmò, Palace Regular Attendant.
On the wùshēn day,
Yǎn, King of Chángshān, was appointed Grand Chancellor, Commander-in-Chief of all military forces inside and outside the court, and Overseer of the Affairs of the Department of State Affairs.
Zhàn, Grand Marshal
and King of Chángguǎng, was appointed Grand Tutor and Grand Commander of the Capital Region.
Duàn Sháo, Minister of Works, was appointed Grand General.
Yān, former Minister of Works and King of Píngyáng, was appointed Grand Commandant.
Guīyàn, Minister of Works and King of Píngqín, was appointed Minister of Works (Sītú).
Yóu, King of Péngchéng, was appointed Minister of State Affairs.
Furthermore, Tāng, Crown Prince of Gāolí, was appointed Envoy with Staff, concurrently Commander of the Eastern Barbarians, Duke of Liáodōng Commandery, and King of Gāolí.
In this month,
Wáng Lín was defeated by Chén,
and Xiāo Zhuāng fled to Hézhōu.
In the third month, on the jiǎyín day,
an edict ordered that all military and state affairs be reported to Jìnyáng
and subject to the calculations and plans of Grand Chancellor Yǎn, King of Chángshān.
On the rénshēn day,
Xiàohéng, the second son of Wénxiāng, was enfeoffed as King of Guǎngníng.
Chánggōng, his third son, was enfeoffed as King of Lánlíng.
Summer, fourth month, on the guǐhài day,
an edict stated that in the nine provinces of Hénán, Dìng, Jì, Zhào, Yíng, Cāng, Nánjiāo, Guāng, and Qīng,
due to a locust plague,
the seasonal crops were quite damaged.
Envoys were dispatched on different routes to provide relief.
In this month,
Emperor Míng of Zhōu passed away.
Fifth month, on the rénzǐ day,
Liú Hónghuī, Open-Commission-Holder with the Rank of Three Grand Ministers, was appointed Right Grand Secretary of the Department of State Affairs.
Autumn, eighth month, on the rénwǔ day,
the Grand Empress Dowager ordered the deposed emperor to be made King of Jìnán,
and to be granted one commandery for his sustenance.
Yǎn, Grand Chancellor and King of Chángshān, was to accede to the grand succession.
On that day,
the King resided in a separate palace.
In the ninth month of the second year of Huángjiàn,
he died in Jìnyáng,
aged seventeen.
The Emperor was intelligent and mature from an early age,
generous, benevolent, and wise.
During the Tiānbǎo era, he had an excellent reputation.
When he assumed the great position,
Yáng Yīn, Yàn Zǐxiàn, Sòng Qīndào, and others jointly assisted him.
Because King of Chángshān was a close relative and highly respected,
feared and admired by all,
and moreover, on the day Wénxuān first passed away,
the Empress Dowager had originally intended to establish him [as emperor],
Yīn and others harbored suspicions and jealousy.
The King of Chángshān was worried and displeased,
so he reported to the Empress Dowager to execute their faction.
At that time, Guīyàn, King of Píngqín, was also privy to the plot.
In the autumn of the second year of Huángjiàn,
celestial phenomena indicated a change.
Guīyàn feared future harm,
so he reported to Xiàozhāo [that]
the King would be to blame.
Thus, Guīyàn was dispatched by express courier to the Jìnyáng Palace to kill him.
After the King's death,
Xiàozhāo fell ill,
seeing Wénxuān's ghost tormenting him.
Xiàozhāo deeply detested this,
and despite employing all methods of exorcism, it was to no avail.
Thirty days after his death, Xiàozhāo passed away.
In the second year of Dàníng,
he was buried northwest of Wǔníng,
and was posthumously named King Mǐndào.
Initially, Wénxuān ordered Xíng Shào to devise the Emperor's given name as Yīn and his courtesy name as Zhèngdào.
The Emperor followed up by criticizing him, saying:
"The Yīn dynasty was known for fraternal succession.
The character 'zhèng' (正)
is composed of 'yī' (一) and 'zhǐ' (止).
My children will not succeed me after my death."
Shào was frightened
and requested a change.
Wénxuān did not permit it, saying:
"It is fate."
He then said to Emperor Xiàozhāo:
"You may depose him,
but be careful not to kill him."
Collator's Notes
Annals Six, Xiàozhāo
Emperor Xiàozhāo Yǎn,
courtesy name Yán'ān,
was the sixth son of Emperor Shénwǔ
and the younger brother of Emperor Wénxuān by the same mother.
He was brilliant and extraordinary in his youth,
and early on showed signs of great accomplishments.
Empress Dowager Wǔmíng loved and esteemed him greatly.
In the first year of Yuánxiàng of Wèi,
he was enfeoffed as Duke of Chángshān Commandery.
When Wénxiāng governed,
he sent Lǐ Tóngguǐ, Central Secretariat Attendant, to the princely residence to be a tutor to his younger brothers.
The Emperor, when perusing texts,
delved into their essence and meaning, rather than focusing on flowery language.
He often sighed, saying:
"Though the masters of Méngjīn,
the left horse shivered but did not flinch."
He considered this to be competence.
He then devoted himself to reading the Hàng Shū,
and upon reaching the biography of Lǐ Líng,
he admired his actions.
He was exceptionally intelligent;
when interacting with others,
once he knew their family taboos,
he never inadvertently violated them throughout his life.
When Tóngguǐ fell ill and died,
Diāo Ròu, who was a Changliu Canjun of the Kaifu, was ordered to replace him.
He was stern and narrow-minded by nature,
unsuitable for gentle guidance and instruction,
and was dismissed midway.
When the Emperor saw him off from his residence,
he looked grim and solemn,
with tears streaming down his face in several lines.
Those around him could not help but sigh in grief.
Such was his respect for his profession and his old acquaintances.
At the beginning of Tiānbǎo,
his rank was elevated to King.
In the fifth year,
he was appointed Minister of State Affairs concurrently of Bīng Province.
The Emperor was adept at making decisions
and skilled in managing affairs,
and all within the Department of State Affairs feared and obeyed him.
In the seventh year,
he followed Wénxuān back to Yè.
Wénxuān, finding many discrepancies in the memorials submitted by the Department of State Affairs,
ordered the Emperor to first discuss and settle the merits and demerits with the court officials,
and only then present them.
The Emperor was skilled in political tactics,
and his judgments were always sound and logical.
Wénxuān greatly admired him.
In the eighth year,
he was transferred to Minister of Works (Sīkōng) and Overseer of the Affairs of the Department of State Affairs.
In the ninth year,
he was appointed Grand Marshal,
and still Overseer of the Affairs of the Department of State Affairs.
Gāo Xiàowǎn (孝琬), being the legitimate eldest son of Wénxiāng (文襄),
was arrogant and conceited.
When the King of Hénán (河南王) died,
none of the princes in the palace dared to speak out,
only Gāo Xiàowǎn (孝琬) cried loudly and exited.
He also resented the powerful officials,
making a straw man and shooting arrows at it.
Hé Shìkāi (和士開) and Zǔ Tǐng (祖珽) slandered him,
saying:
"The straw man represents Your Sacred Person.
Also, earlier when the Tujue (突厥) arrived at the prefecture,
Gāo Xiàowǎn (孝琬) took off his helmet and threw it to the ground,
saying 'Am I an old woman
who needs to wear this?'
These words referred to the empress dowager."
Initially,
there was a rumor in the Wèi (魏) era:
"Grain planted in Hénán (河南) grows in Héběi (河北),
a golden rooster crows on a white poplar tree."
Zǔ Tǐng (祖珽) explained it thus:
"Hénán (河南) and Héběi (河北)
refer to Héjiān (河間).
The golden rooster crowing means
Gāo Xiàowǎn (孝琬) will establish the golden rooster and grant a general amnesty."
The Emperor was somewhat misled by this.
At that time, Gāo Xiàowǎn (孝琬) obtained a Buddha tooth,
which he placed in his residence,
and at night it emitted divine light.
Zhāoxuán Dū Fǎshùn (昭玄都法順) requested to report this to the throne,
but Gāo Xiàowǎn (孝琬) did not agree.
When the Emperor heard of it,
he ordered a search,
and hundreds of spears and banners for guarding the treasury were found.
When the Emperor heard of this,
he considered it an act of rebellion.
He interrogated Gāo Xiàowǎn's (孝琬) concubines;
one named Chén (陳), who was out of favor,
falsely replied
"Gāo Xiàowǎn (孝琬) drew a likeness of Your Majesty and cried over it,"
but in reality, it was an image of Wénxiāng (文襄),
and Gāo Xiàowǎn (孝琬) often wept before it.
The Emperor was enraged,
and ordered Wǔwèi Hèlián Fǔxuán (武衞赫連輔玄) to flog him with a reverse whip.
Gāo Xiàowǎn (孝琬) called out "Uncle,"
the Emperor angrily said:
"Who is your uncle?
How dare you call me uncle!"
Gāo Xiàowǎn (孝琬) said:
"As the legitimate grandson of Shénwǔ Huángdì (神武皇帝),
the legitimate son of Wénxiāng Huángdì (文襄皇帝),
and the maternal nephew of Wèi Xiàojìng Huángdì (魏孝靜皇帝),
why can I not call you uncle?"
The Emperor became even more furious,
broke both his shins, and he died.
He was buried in the Western Hills;
after the Emperor's demise,
he was reburied.
His son Zhèng Lǐ (正禮) succeeded him;
he was intelligent and bright in his youth,
and could recite the Zuǒshì Chūnqiū (左氏春秋).
When Qí (齊) fell,
he was moved to Miánzhōu (綿州) where he died.
Lánlíng Wǔ Wáng Gāo Chánggōng (蘭陵武王長恭),
also named Gāo Xiàoguàn (孝瓘),
was the fourth son of Wénxiāng (文襄).
He successively served as Píngzhōu Cìshǐ (幷州刺史).
When the Tujue (突厥) invaded Jìnyáng (晉陽),
Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) fought with all his might against them.
During the defeat at Mángshān (芒山),
Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) led the central army,
and with five hundred cavalry, he re-entered the Zhōu (周) army's lines,
then reached below Jīnyǒng (金墉).
Being severely besieged,
the people on the city wall did not recognize him,
so Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) removed his helmet to show his face,
and then crossbowmen were sent down to rescue him,
resulting in a great victory.
The warriors together sang a song about him,
which is the "Lánlíng Wáng Rùzhèn Qǔ" (蘭陵王入陣曲).
He successively held posts as Sīzhōu Mù (司州牧) and governor of Qīng (青) and Yíng (瀛) prefectures,
and accepted quite a lot of wealth.
Later he became Tàiwèi (太尉),
and with Duàn Sháo (段韶) he attacked Bǎigǔ (栢谷),
and also assaulted Dìngyáng (定陽).
When Duàn Sháo (韶) fell ill,
Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) took command of his troops.
For his military achievements, he was successively enfeoffed as Duke of Jùlù (鉅鹿), Chánglè (長樂), Lèpíng (樂平), and Gāoyáng (高陽) commanderies.
After the victory at Mángshān (芒山),
the Later Emperor said to Gāo Chánggōng (長恭):
"You entered the lines too deeply;
if you had suffered a defeat, you would have regretted it too late."
He replied:
"It was a family matter and urgent,
so I didn't realize it."
The Emperor disliked his referring to it as a "family matter,"
and thus grew wary of him.
When he was in Dìngyáng (定陽),
his subordinate Wèi Xiāngyuàn (尉相願) said to him:
"Since Your Highness has received the court's trust,
how can you be so greedy and cruel?"
Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) did not answer.
Wèi Xiāngyuàn (相願) said:
"Is it not because of the great victory at Mángshān (芒山),
that you fear being envied for your prestige and might,
and wish to defile yourself?"
Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) said:
"Indeed."
Wèi Xiāngyuàn (相願) said:
"If the court truly envies Your Highness,
committing this offense will certainly incur punishment;
seeking fortune will instead hasten disaster."
Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) wept,
knelt forward and asked for a method to ensure his safety.
Wèi Xiāngyuàn (相願) said:
"Your Highness already has achievements from before,
and now you have reported another victory;
your prestige and renown are too great.
You should feign illness and stay at home,
not getting involved in affairs."
Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) thought his words were right,
but was unable to retire.
When Jianghuai (江淮) was plagued by bandits,
he feared being made a general again,
and sighed:
"My face was swollen last year;
why does it not flare up now?"
From then on, he suffered from illness but did not seek treatment.
In the fifth month of the fourth year of Wǔpíng (武平)
the Emperor sent Xú Zhīfàn (徐之範) to give him poisoned wine.
Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) said to his consort, Lady Zhèng (鄭氏):
"I served my sovereign loyally;
what sin have I committed against Heaven
to suffer poisoning?"
His consort said:
"Why not request an audience with His Majesty?"
Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) said:
"How can I gain an audience with His Majesty?"
He then drank the poison and died.
He was posthumously granted the title of Tàiwèi (太尉).
Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) had a gentle appearance but a strong heart,
and possessed both a beautiful voice and countenance.
As a general, he was diligent in minor matters,
and whenever he received delicacies,
even a single melon or a few fruits,
he would certainly share them with his officers and soldiers.
When he was first in Yíngzhōu (瀛州),
his staff officer Yáng Shìshēn (陽士深) impeached him for corruption,
and he was dismissed from office.
Later, when attacking Dìngyáng (定陽),
Yáng Shìshēn (士深) was in the army,
and feared that misfortune would befall him.
Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) heard of this and said:
"I never had such an intention."
He then sought a minor fault,
and had Yáng Shìshēn (士深) flogged twenty times with a rod to reassure him.
Once, he went to court, and his retainers all dispersed,
with only one remaining;
Gāo Chánggōng (長恭) returned alone,
without scolding or punishing anyone.
Wǔchéng (武成) rewarded his merits,
ordering Jiǎ Hù (賈護) to buy twenty concubines for him,
but he only accepted one.
He had a debt bond for a thousand pieces of gold;
on the day of his death,
he burned them all.
Ān Dé Wáng Yánzōng
was the fifth son of Wénxiāng.
His mother, Lady Chén,
was a courtesan of Guǎngyáng Wáng.
Yánzōng was raised by Wénxuān from a young age.
When he was twelve,
Wénxuān still had him ride on his belly,
letting him urinate into his navel,
and hugging him, said:
“It is pitiful that I only have this one.”
He asked what king he wanted to be,
and Yánzōng replied:
“I wish to be Chōngtiān Wáng.”
Wénxuān asked Yáng Yīn,
who said:
“There is no such commandery name in the world.
I wish for him to be at peace with virtue (ān yú dé).”
Thereupon, he was enfeoffed as Ān Dé Wáng.
When he was the Cìshǐ of Dìngzhōu,
he defecated from an upper story,
making people below open their mouths to receive it.
He mixed steamed pork with human feces to feed his attendants,
and those who showed reluctance were whipped.
When Xiàozhāo Dì heard of this,
he sent Zhào Dàodé to the prefecture to whip him one hundred times.
Dàodé, seeing that Yánzōng did not receive the flogging with proper respect,
added thirty more blows.
He also used prisoners to test swords,
to examine their sharpness or dullness.
He was arrogant, indulgent, and committed many unlawful acts.
Wǔchéng had him flogged,
and killed nine of his close attendants.
From then on, he deeply reformed himself.
When Lánlíng Wáng achieved victory at Mángshān,
he boasted of his military might,
and all his brothers admired him.
Yánzōng alone said:
“The fourth brother is no true hero.
Why did he not press on with the victory and directly enter?
If Yánzōng were in that position,
how could Guānxī possibly still exist?”
When Lánlíng died,
his consort, Lady Zhèng, donated her pearl necklace to the Buddha.
Guǎngníng Wáng tried to redeem it.
Yánzōng wrote a letter to remonstrate,
and his tears filled the paper.
When Héjiān died,
Yánzōng also cried many tears.
He also made a straw figure in the likeness of Wǔchéng,
whipped it, and questioned it, saying:
“Why did you kill my brother!”
His servant reported this,
and Wǔchéng pinned Yánzōng to the ground,
flogged him two hundred times with a horsewhip,
nearly killing him.
Later, he successively held the posts of Sītú and Tàiwèi.
During the campaign of Píngyáng,
the Hòuzhǔ personally commanded,
ordering Yánzōng to lead the right army to fight first,
capturing Zhōu Kāifǔ Zōngtǐng outside the city.
During the great battle,
Yánzōng, with his subordinates, entered the Zhōu army twice,
and none failed to be scattered.
While all other armies were defeated,
Yánzōng alone preserved his entire army.
When the Hòuzhǔ was about to flee to Jìnyáng,
Yánzōng said:
“Your Majesty, just stay in the camp and do not move.
Entrust the troops to your servant,
and your servant can defeat them.”
The Emperor did not accept this.
When he arrived at Bīngzhōu,
and further heard that the Zhōu army had already entered Quèshǔ Gǔ,
he then appointed Yánzōng as Xiàngguó and Bīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
to take overall command of the military affairs of Shānxī.
He said:
“Bīngzhōu, brother, you take it for yourself.
I am leaving now.”
Yánzōng said:
“Your Majesty, for the sake of the altars of soil and grain, do not move.
Your servant will fight with all his might for Your Majesty.”
Luò Típó said:
“The Supreme One’s plan is already decided,
Your Highness must not obstruct it.”
The Hòuzhǔ ultimately fled to Yè.
The generals and officers in Bīngzhōu all pleaded, saying:
“If Your Highness does not become the Son of Heaven,
we truly cannot fight with all our might.”
Yánzōng, having no choice,
ascended the imperial throne,
and issued an edict saying:
“Wǔpíng is weak,
the government is controlled by eunuchs,
strife is within the inner court,
and bandits rise on the frontiers.
Breaking through the passes and fleeing by night,
his whereabouts unknown,
the enterprise of our High Ancestor will fall to the ground.
The princes, dukes, ministers, and officials
