have earnestly urged and compelled me;
I now respectfully assume the revered position.
Let there be a great amnesty throughout the realm,
and change the seventh year of Wǔpíng to the first year of Déchāng.”
He appointed Jìnchāng Wáng Táng Yōng as prime minister,
Qíchāng Wáng Mòduōlóu Jìngxiǎn, Shùyáng Wáng Hé'ā Yúzǐ,
the Right Protector-General Duàn Chàng, Wǔwèi General Xiānglǐ Sēngjiā, Kāifǔ Hán Gǔhú, and Hóumòchén Luòzhōu as his close aides.
When the people heard of this,
those who came without being summoned
followed one after another.
Yánzōng was physically robust;
when sitting, he leaned back,
when lying down, he lay prostrate.
People laughed at him,
but then he would rise up with a roar.
His strength was extraordinary,
and he galloped through battle formations,
swift and agile as if flying.
He emptied the treasuries and the beautiful women of the imperial harem,
distributing them to his generals and soldiers,
and confiscated over a thousand households of inner attendants.
The Hòuzhǔ said to his close ministers:
“I would rather the Zhōu obtain Bīngzhōu
than Ān Dé obtain it.”
His attendants said:
“That is reasonable.”
When Yánzōng saw the soldiers,
he personally held their hands,
stated his name and expressed his resolve,
weeping and sobbing.
Everyone vied to die for him;
even children and women climbed onto roofs, bared their arms,
and threw bricks and stones to resist the Zhōu army.
The Tèjìn and Kāifǔ, Nàlú Ānshēng, who was defending Tàigǔ,
rebelled with ten thousand troops.
The Zhōu army besieged Jìnyáng,
appearing like black clouds gathering from all four directions.
Yánzōng ordered Mòduōlóu Jìngxiǎn and Hán Gǔhú to defend the south of the city,
and Hé'ā Yúzǐ and Duàn Chàng to defend the east of the city.
Yánzōng personally confronted Zhōu Qí Wáng north of the city,
wielding a great spear,
going back and forth supervising the battle,
sweeping away all in his path.
The Shàngshū Lìshǐ Jǔshān was also large and strong,
and followed on foot, wielding a long saber,
killing and wounding many.
Wǔwèi Lán Fúróng and Qílián Yáncháng both died in battle.
In the early Tiānpíng reign,
Téng entered as Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè.
Of all matters, internal and external,
Téng was thoroughly aware.
He also held the concurrent titles of Sīkōng and Shàngshū Lìng.
At that time, the Western Wèi dispatched generals to raid Nányān Commandery.
An imperial edict appointed Téng as Nándào Xíngtái,
leading various generals to suppress them.
Téng was by nature timid
and lacked strategic prowess,
suffering a defeat and returning.
He was then appointed Sītú.
Initially, when the northern frontier was in chaos,
he lost a daughter.
After he became prominent,
he made extensive inquiries from afar,
but ultimately failed to find her,
suspecting she had become a lowly maidservant.
When he became Sītú,
regarding those who sued for their freedom from servitude,
he did not investigate the truth,
but generally freed them.
He wished to free a thousand people,
hoping to find his daughter among them.
At that time, Gāozǔ entered the court,
and some attendants spoke of this.
Gāozǔ was greatly enraged
and dismissed him from his position as Sītú.
During the Wǔdìng reign,
he was sent to Qīngzhōu
to investigate and register fugitive households.
He was then promoted to Tàibǎo.
Initially, Cuī Xiàofēn of Bólíng adopted a poor family's daughter named Jiǎ as his foster daughter.
After Xiàofēn died,
his wife Yuán remarried Zhèng Bóyóu
and brought Jiǎ with her to the Zhèng family.
Jiǎ possessed beauty,
and Téng took her in.
Initially, she was his concubine.
When his wife, Lady Yuán, died,
Téng, because Jiǎ had a son,
formally made her his wife.
An imperial edict enfeoffed her as Dānyáng Jùnjūn.
He further requested that the title of Lady Yuán be transferred to his daughter.
Such disregard for rites and indulgence of personal desires
were common for him.
Téng had early on attached himself to Gāozǔ.
Through hardship and peril,
he diligently and respectfully served,
earning deep trust and favor.
When Gāozǔ established him in the Wèi court,
entrusting him as a confidant,
his ambition and arrogance swelled.
He had the power to grant and seize as he pleased.
He sought and accepted bribes
without limit.
Appointments in life and posthumous honors in death
did not pass without payment.
He concealed silver vessels,
stealing them for his own household.
He befriended petty men
and specialized in extortion.
In Yè,
he, Gāo Yuè, Gāo Lóngzhī, and Sīmǎ Zǐrú were known as the Four Nobles.
They wantonly abused their power,
and Téng was the worst of them.
Gāozǔ repeatedly censured him,
but he never repented.
The court and public deeply scorned him.
In the fourth month of Wǔdìng 6, he passed away
at the age of sixty-eight.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Jì Dìng děng Wǔ Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì, Jìzhōu Cìshǐ, Tàishī, Kāifǔ, and Lùshàngshūshì.
His posthumous name was Wén.
In the early Tiānbǎo reign,
due to Téng's assistance in establishing the dynasty,
an imperial edict ordered a sacrifice at his tomb.
During the Huángjiàn reign,
he was enshrined in Gāozǔ's ancestral temple.
His son Fèngzhēn inherited his title.
Fèngzhēn was mediocre and dull.
During the Wǔpíng reign,
he died holding the rank of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Gāo Lóngzhī,
courtesy name Yánxīng,
originally bore the surname Xú.
He claimed descent from Gāopíng Jīnxiāng.
His father Gàn,
Wèi Bái Shuǐ Jùnshǒu,
was adopted by his paternal aunt's husband, the Gāo family,
and thus adopted their surname.
When Lóngzhī became prominent,
the Wèi court posthumously granted Gàn the titles of Sītú Gōng and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Later, Lóngzhī contributed to policy discussions,
and Gāozǔ ordered him to be considered a younger cousin,
stating he was from Bóhǎi Xiū.
Lóngzhī was eight feet tall,
had a handsome beard,
and was profound and ambitious.
When Yuè, Prince of Rúnán, was Sīzhōu Mù,
he appointed Lóngzhī as Hùcáo Cóngshì.
In the early Jiànyì reign,
he was appointed Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì without formal examination.
He went out with Xíngtái Yú Huī to suppress Yáng Kǎn in Tàishān.
Huī appointed Lóngzhī as Xíngtái Lángzhōng,
and he was also appointed Gěishìzhōng.
He formed a deep bond with Gāozǔ.
When Gāozǔ took charge of Jìnzhōu,
he appointed Lóngzhī as Zhìzhōng,
acting as Píngyáng Jùnshì.
He followed Gāozǔ in his uprising in Shāndōng,
and was appointed Dàxíngtái Yòuchéng.
In the early Wèi Zhōngxīng reign,
he was appointed Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi,
also holding the post of Shàngshí Diǎnyù.
He followed Gāozǔ in pacifying Yè,
acting as Xiāngzhōu Shì.
He followed in defeating the Four Hú at Hánlíng.
In the early Tàichāng reign,
he was appointed Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn and Yítóng Sānsī.
Emperor Wén of Western Wèi once had a heated argument with Lóngzhī due to wine.
Emperor Wén was subsequently dismissed and demoted.
Gāozǔ criticized Lóngzhī for his inability to maintain harmony,
and then proposed that he be sent out as Běidào Xíngtái.
He was then transferred to be Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ,
enfeoffed as Píngyuán Jùngōng,
with a stipend of one thousand seven hundred households.
Lóngzhī requested a reduction of seven hundred households
and also asked to be demoted by four ranks to yield to his elder brother Téng.
An imperial edict graciously permitted this,
and Téng was then made Cāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
When Gāozǔ campaigned against Húxī Chūn,
he appointed Lóngzhī as Dàxíngtái Shàngshū.
When Dàsīmǎ and Qīnghé Wáng Dǎn held power,
Lóngzhī was appointed Shìzhōng, Shàngshū Yòupúyè,
and concurrently Yùshǐ Zhōngwèi.
He extensively employed laborers
to construct grand temples and pagodas,
for which he was reprimanded by Gāozǔ.
In the early Tiānpíng reign,
he resigned due to his mother's mourning.
Soon, an imperial edict appointed him Bìngzhōu Cìshǐ,
and he later entered as Shàngshū Yòupúyè.
At that time, when land was first distributed to the people,
the powerful and influential all occupied the fertile and beautiful fields,
while the poor and weak received only barren plots.
Lóngzhī memorialized Gāozǔ,
requesting a complete reversal and redistribution,
and thus fairness was achieved.
He also concurrently served as Yínggòu Dàjiàng.
All construction in the capital city
was overseen by him.
He extended the southern city wall to a circumference of twenty-five *lǐ*.
Because the Zhāng River was close to the imperial city,
he built a long dike to prevent the danger of flooding.
He also dug canals to divert the Zhāng River to flow around the city,
and constructed water mills,
all of which were beneficial at the time.
From the Xiàochāng reign onwards,
the Wèi dynasty faced many difficulties.
Cìshǐ and Tàishǒu all became Dūdū of their respective departments.
Even without military affairs,
they all appointed assistant officials,
which caused considerable vexation in various localities.
Lóngzhī memorialized, requesting that,
unless they were truly in border vital areas
and had existing troops,
all such appointments should be abolished.
Furthermore, many court nobles falsely assumed the title of Chángshì to obtain the adornments of mink and cicada.
Lóngzhī himself submitted a memorial to resign as Shìzhōng,
and also stated that all those who falsely wore the attire of Chángshì
should also be dismissed.
The imperial edict granted all his requests.
Since the state had many military and governmental affairs,
those who falsely claimed titles and usurped offices were countless.
Lóngzhī memorialized to investigate them,
finding over fifty thousand people.
However, the crowd of petty individuals clamored,
and Lóngzhī, fearing them, stopped.
An imperial edict appointed him Jiānjǐqíjūshì
and promoted him to Sītú Gōng.
During the Wǔdìng reign,
he served as Héběi Kuòhù Dàshǐ.
He was recalled
and appointed Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn and Lùshàngshūshì,
soon also holding the concurrent title of Shìzhōng.
He then served as acting Qīngzhōu Shì.
He was recalled
and appointed Tàizǐ Tàishī, concurrently Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè, and Lìbù Shàngshū.
He was then promoted to Tàibǎo.
At that time, Shìzōng was in charge of governance,
and customs were strictly purified.
Lóngzhī sometimes accepted bribes,
for which Shìzōng severely reprimanded and humiliated him in the Shàngshū Shěng.
When Qí received the abdication,
he was promoted in rank to King.
Soon after, he was appointed to his original post as Commissioner of the Secretariat,
Great Superintendent of the Imperial Clan,
and Supervisor of National History.
Lóngzhī's nature was somewhat petty and fond of novelty.
As for the imperial regalia, various entertainments, and dress codes for the government, he often made changes,
not following established precedents.
Contemporary opinion criticized him for this.
On the archery target mound, he erected three human statues in a posture of valor and strength.
Xiǎnzǔ once visited Dōngshān,
and while shooting, he said to Lóngzhī:
"On the archery target mound, fierce beasts should be depicted
to preserve the ancient meaning.
Why place human figures?
Shooting at humans all day
is something I do not approve of."
Lóngzhī had no reply.
Initially, Shìzōng had entrusted affairs to Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat Cuī Xiān and Imperial Household Attendant Cuī Jìshū, among others.
When Shìzōng passed away,
Lóngzhī petitioned Xiǎnzǔ, wishing to harm them all,
but was not permitted.
Xiǎnzǔ, considering Lóngzhī an old acquaintance,
entrusted him with government affairs.
Jìshū and others, holding onto previous grievances,
then slandered him, saying:
"Whenever Lóngzhī sees a litigant,
he invariably shows pity and compassion,
to indicate that he is not capable of arbitrating."
Xiǎnzǔ thought that since he had been entrusted with such heavy responsibilities,
and knew of the injustice,
he should have rectified it appropriately.
How could he shirk responsibility and seek fame?
This was not the duty of a great minister.
In the fifth year of Tiānbǎo (554),
he was prohibited from the Department of the Imperial Secretariat.
Lóngzhī once feasted and drank with Yuán Chǎng.
When the wine was flowing freely,
he said to Chǎng:
"When befriending a king,
one should not betray him in life or death."
Someone secretly reported this.
Furthermore, before the Emperor ascended the throne,
Lóngzhī often harbored contempt for him.
When the Emperor was about to receive the abdication from Wèi,
all the great ministers said it was not yet time,
The Emperor held a deep grudge against him.
Because of this,
he then erupted in great anger,
ordering strongmen to beat him over a hundred times.
When he was released,
thirsty, he was about to drink water,
but someone stopped him.
Lóngzhī said:
"What does today matter!"
and then drank.
Subsequently, he followed the imperial carriage
and died on the road,
at the age of sixty-one.

He was posthumously granted the titles of Commander of Military Affairs for the Five Prefectures of Jì, Dìng, Yíng, Cāng, and Yōu; Grand General; Grand Commandant; Grand Protector; and Governor of Jì Prefecture;
and Prince of Yángxià.
He ultimately did not receive a posthumous title.
Although Lóngzhī was not well-versed in scholarship,
he admired and esteemed literary elegance.
He always treated gentry and literati
with proper courtesy.
His widowed elder sister was a nun,
and he served her as he would his mother.
In instructing and supervising his sons,
he always prioritized literature and righteousness.
The world greatly praised him for this.
In Xiǎnzǔ's later years,
as he became increasingly suspicious and cruel,
he remembered his resentment towards Lóngzhī,
and executed more than ten of his sons, including Déshū,
and threw them all into the Zhāng River.
He also desecrated Lóngzhī's tomb,
exhumed his corpse –
which had been buried for many years,
but its appearance had not changed –
hacked and cut his bones,
and also cast them into the Zhāng River,
thus ending his lineage.
During the Qiánmíng era (560),
an imperial edict appointed his elder brother's son, Zǐyuǎn, as Lóngzhī's successor,
to inherit the title of Prince of Yángxià,
and returned his property.
Initially,
Lóngzhī, trusting Gāozǔ,
was inherently insidious and malicious.
He never failed to retaliate
for even the smallest grievance.
When Grandee Secretary Cuī Xiàofēn failed to secure a marriage alliance with him,
and Grand Minister of the Imperial Treasury Rèn Jí, while jointly supervising construction,
had some disagreements with him,
and Governor of Yíng Prefecture Yuán Yàn's solicitations were not successful,
he subsequently fabricated charges against them,
and had them all executed.
In the end, his own family was annihilated.
Commentators said that this was retribution.
Sīmǎ Zǐrú,
courtesy name Zūnyè,
was a native of Wēn, Hénèi.
His eighth-generation ancestor, Mó,
was Grand Commandant and Prince of Nányáng in the Jìn dynasty.
Mó's heir, Bǎo,
fled to Liángzhōu during the Jìn disturbances
and settled there.
When Wèi pacified Gūzāng,
they moved to Yúnzhōng,
as his autobiography states.
His father, Xīnglóng,
was Administrator of Lǔyáng for Wèi.
Zǐrú was astute and quick-witted in his youth,
eloquent,
and enjoyed befriending heroes.
He formed a deep bond
of righteousness with Gāozǔ.
During the Xiàochāng era (525-528),
when the northern provinces fell,
Zǐrú took his family south to Sìzhōu,
where he was treated with courtesy by Ěrzhū Róng,
who granted him command of the Central Army.
When Róng marched towards Luò,
he appointed Zǐrú as Sīmǎ,
with credentials, acting General Who Pacifies the South,
and Supervisor of the Vanguard.
Upon reaching Gāodū,
Róng, fearing that Jiànxīng's treacherous terrain
and crucial location for passage
would pose a threat to his rear,
appointed Zǐrú as acting Administrator of Jiànxīng and Area Commander of that commandery.
In the early Yǒng'ān era (528),
he was enfeoffed as a County Baron of Píngyáo,
with three hundred households,
and remained as a Supervising Secretary of the Grand Imperial Secretariat.
Róng, recognizing Zǐrú's eloquence
and ability to explain current affairs,
frequently dispatched him as an envoy to the court.
He often pleased the emperor,
and Xiàozhuāng also received him courteously.
During Gě Róng's rebellion,
Xiāngzhōu was isolated and precarious.
Róng sent Zǐrú through enemy lines to Yè,
to assist in its defense.
After Gě Róng was pacified,
he was promoted in rank to Marquis.
When Yuán Hào entered Luò,
people's hearts were divided.
Knowing that Zǐrú had once defended Yè City
and had considerable prestige,
he appointed him to act as Governor of Xiāng Prefecture.
After Hào was pacified,
he was summoned to be Grand Master of Radiance with Golden Seals and Purple Ribbons.
When Ěrzhū Róng was executed,
Zǐrú, knowing of the coup,
rushed out of the palace,
went to Róng's residence,
abandoned his family, and fled the capital with Róng's wife and Ěrzhū Shìlóng, among others.
Shìlóng immediately wished to return north.
Zǐrú said:
"In affairs, it is crucial to respond to opportunity.
In warfare, deceit is not disdained.
The world is in turmoil,
and only the strong are observed.
At this critical juncture,
we cannot show weakness.
If we must flee north,
I fear that unforeseen changes will arise.
It is better to divide our troops to guard the river bridge,
turn our army back towards the capital,
and take them by surprise.
Perhaps they will collapse.
Even if it doesn't go as we wish,
it will still be enough to show that we have remaining strength,
and make the world observe and listen,
fearing our might."
Thereupon, Shìlóng returned and pressed upon the capital.
Wèi appointed Prince of Chángguǎng and Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
The former deposed emperor appointed him as Attendant at Court, General of Agile Cavalry, Grandee Secretary,
and advanced his peerage to Duke of Yángpíng Commandery,
with one thousand seven hundred households.
He firmly declined the title of Grandee Secretary.
When Gāozǔ raised an army in Xìndū,
Shìlóng and others, knowing Zǐrú's old ties with Gāozǔ,
became suspicious
and sent him out as Governor of Nánqí Prefecture.
Zǐrú was indignant,
wept and pleaded his case,
but was not spared.
Ěrzhū (爾朱) was defeated.
Yǔ (與) and Yùzhōu (豫州) Cìshǐ (刺史) Lǐ Ēn (李恩) returned to Gāozǔ (高祖).
For his merits, he was repeatedly promoted to Āndōng Jiāngjūn (安東將軍) and Gāoliáng Tàishǒu (高梁太守).
[二二] He was transferred to Wǔchéng Tàishǒu (五城太守) and Dōngyōngzhōu Cìshǐ (東雍州刺史).
At the defeat of Shāyuàn (沙苑),
the Western Wèi (西魏) Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ (荊州刺史) Guō Luán (郭鸞) led his troops to attack Yǎn (儼).
He resisted the siege for over two hundred days,
fighting day and night with all his might,
and severely defeated Luán’s (鸞) army.
He pursued and decapitated over three hundred enemy soldiers,
and also captured the Western Wèi (西魏) Cìshǐ (刺史) Guō Tā (郭他).
At that time, many prefectures had defected or fallen,
but only Yǎn (儼) remained intact.
He was promoted to Zhènnán Jiāngjūn (鎮南將軍).
In the third year of Wǔdìng (武定) [545 CE],
he led an army to relieve the siege of Xiāngzhōu (襄州).
He frequently served as an envoy to Rúróu (茹茹).
He also participated in the attack on Yùbì (玉壁),
and was bestowed with seven hundred bolts of silk, along with clothing and hats.
In the fifth year [547 CE],
he garrisoned Héquiáo (河橋) and Wǔchéng (五城).
When Hóu Jǐng (侯景) rebelled,
Yǎn (儼) attacked the bandits of Chénjùn (陳郡),

capturing Qùdí Hélài (厙狄曷賴) from Jǐng’s (景) command, as well as the falsely appointed Tàishǒu (太守) Zhèng Dàohé (鄭道合), Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ (兗州刺史) Wáng Yànxià (王彥夏), and Xíngtái (行臺) Dí Chàng (狄暢), among others.
He captured and killed over a hundred enemy soldiers.
When he returned to Xiàngchéng (項城),
he again captured Jǐng’s (景) falsely appointed Cìshǐ (刺史) Xīn Guāng (辛光) and Cài Zūn (蔡遵),
along with two thousand of their subordinates.
In the sixth year [548 CE],
he was appointed Qiáozhōu Cìshǐ (譙州刺史).
He frequently achieved military successes,
and many surrendered and submitted to him.
In the seventh year [549 CE],
he was again appointed Jiāozhōu Cìshǐ (膠州刺史).
At the beginning of Tiānbǎo (天保) [550 CE],
he was appointed Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司).
In the sixth year [555 CE],
Liáng (梁) Sītú (司徒) Lù Fǎhé (陸法和) and Yítóng (儀同) Sòng Chǎi (宋茝), among others, led their subordinates and offered the city of Yǐngzhōu (郢州) in surrender.
[二三] At that time, Qīnghé Wáng Yuè (清河王岳) led his army along the river.
He then gathered all the generals and deliberated, saying:
“The city is outside the Jiāng (江),
and the people’s morale is still resistant.
We must have someone with both talent and strategy,
and outstanding loyalty and courage,
to be entrusted with this responsibility.”
All unanimously recommended Yǎn (儼).
Yuè (岳) agreed,
and so sent him to garrison Yǐngchéng (郢城).
As soon as he entered,
Hóu Tián (侯瑱) and Rèn Yuē (任約), Grand Commanders of Liáng (梁), immediately led their land and naval forces to the city gates.
Yǎn (儼) deployed defenses in every direction,
and Tián (瑱) and the others could not overcome him.
He also built an extensive pontoon bridge of reeds, several *lǐ* (里) long, upstream at Yīngwǔzhōu (鸚鵡洲),
to block the ship passage.
Communication was cut off,
and the city was isolated and suspended.
The morale of the multitude was fearful.
Yǎn (儼) guided them with loyalty and righteousness,
and also pleased them to calm them.
There was previously a shrine in the city,
popularly known as the Chénghuáng Shén (城隍神) (City God).
Both public and private individuals would pray there.
Therefore, in accordance with the wishes of his officers and soldiers,
he led them to pray,
hoping for divine assistance.
After a short while,
a strong wind suddenly arose,
and surging waves violently stirred,
breaking the reed pontoon bridge.
Yuē (約) again repaired it by linking iron chains,
making the defenses even tighter.
Yǎn (儼) again led the collective prayers,
and a storm arose in the night,
again breaking it apart.
This happened two or three times.
The people in the city were overjoyed,
believing it to be divine assistance.
Tián (瑱) moved his army to the north of the city,
built stockades and set up camps,
and burned down the residential areas outside the city,
destroying all property.
Yuē (約) led over ten thousand warriors,
each carrying siege equipment,
and set up camps and fortifications to the south of the city,
forming a combined force from north and south.
Yǎn (儼) then led his cavalry and infantry out of the city and fiercely attacked,
greatly defeating them,
and capturing over five hundred people.
Previously, Yǐngchéng (郢城) was low-lying,
and its earthen walls were loose and dilapidated.
Yǎn (儼) repaired the city walls and battlements,
and built many tall towers.
He also constructed ships and vessels,
equipping both land and water forces,
with no temporary shortage of workers.
Xiāo Xún (蕭循) also led fifty thousand troops,
and joined forces with Tián (瑱) and Yuē (約),
attacking at night.
Yǎn (儼) and his generals and soldiers fought fiercely all night.
By dawn,
Yuē (約) and the others retreated.
They pursued and decapitated Zhāng Báishí (張白石), a valiant general of Tián (瑱).
Tián (瑱) offered a thousand gold pieces to ransom it,
but Yǎn (儼) refused.
In the fifth month of summer,
Tián (瑱), Yuē (約), and others again combined their forces,
and attacked the city with all their troops.
Food in the city was scarce,
and grain transport was cut off.
There was no plan to remedy this,
and they only ate the leaves of huái (槐) and chǔ (楮) trees, mulberry leaves, jute roots, duckweed, kudzu, mugwort, and other grasses, as well as boots, leather belts, and horn pieces.
When someone died,
their flesh was immediately taken,
divided and eaten by fire,
leaving only the bones.
Yǎn (儼) still issued orders to his generals and soldiers,
ensuring rewards and punishments,
sharing sweet and bitter,
and dedicating their lives to it.
From the first month to the sixth month,
no one harbored dissenting thoughts.
Later, Xiāo Fāngzhì (蕭方智) was enthroned,
and sent an envoy to request peace.
Xiǎnzǔ (顯祖), considering that the city was located south of the Jiāng (江) and inconvenient to hold,
issued an imperial edict to return it.
Yǎn (儼) gazed at the Emperor,
and was overcome with sorrow.
The Emperor called him forward,
held his hand,
touched Yǎn’s (儼) beard and temples,
took off his hat to look at his hair,
and sighed for a long time.
He said to Yǎn (儼):
“Looking at your appearance,
I no longer recognize you.
From ancient times, has any loyal and valiant person
surpassed this!”
Yǎn (儼) replied:
“I relied on Your Majesty’s divine might
to express my foolish integrity,
not bending to the young upstarts,
and again beholding the sacred countenance.
Even if I die tonight,
I will have no regrets in death.”
The Emperor ceaselessly praised him.
He was appointed Zhàozhōu Cìshǐ (趙州刺史),
promoted from Bo (伯) to Gōng (公),
and bestowed with one thousand bolts of silk and one hundred thousand cash.
In the ninth year [558 CE],
he again achieved merit in suppressing bandits,
and was bestowed with one hundred bolts of silk and one hundred thousand cash.
In the tenth year [559 CE],
an imperial edict appointed him Yángzhōu Xíngtái (揚州行臺).
He and Wáng Guìxiǎn (王貴顯) and Hóu Zǐjiān (侯子監) led troops to escort Xiāo Zhuāng (蕭莊).
They built the two cities of Guōmò (郭默) and Ruòxié (若邪).
He fought against Chén (陳) Xīncài Tàishǒu (新蔡太守) Lǔ Xīdá (魯悉達) at Dàshédòng (大蛇洞),
defeating and routing him.
He also supervised Xiāo Zhuāng’s (蕭莊) and Wáng Lín’s (王琳) armies,
and fought against Chén (陳) generals Hóu Tián (侯瑱) and Hóu Āndū (侯安都) at Wúhú (蕪湖),
suffering a defeat.
At the beginning of Huángjiàn (皇建) [560 CE],
he was separately enfeoffed as Chéngyáng Jùngōng (成陽郡公).
In the second year of Tiāntǒng (天統) [566 CE],
he was appointed Tèjìn (特進).
In the tenth month of the fourth year [568 CE],
he was again separately enfeoffed as Yīshì Xiàn Gōng (猗氏縣公),
and also bestowed with one gold and one silver wine cup, and one Hu (胡) horse.
In the fourth month of the fifth year [569 CE],
his noble rank was advanced to Yì'ān Wáng (義安王).

He died during the Wǔpíng 武平 era.
Lú Shúwǔ 盧叔武,
〔一０〕a native of Zhuō 涿 in Fànyáng 范陽,
was the paternal cousin of Qīngzhōu Cìshǐ Wénwěi 青州刺史文偉 (Governor of Qingzhou, Wénwěi).
His father, Guāngzōng 光宗,
had high aspirations.
Shúwǔ 叔武’s two elder brothers, Guān 觀 and Zhòngxuān 仲宣, both distinguished themselves in literature in Luòyáng 洛陽.
Shúwǔ 叔武 was intelligent and quick-witted in his youth,
magnanimous and chivalrous,
and fond of extraordinary strategies.
He admired Zhūgě Liàng 諸葛亮’s character.
He served Hèbá Shèng 賀拔勝 as Jīngzhōu Kāifǔ Chángshǐ 荊州開府長史 (Chief Clerk of the Kaifu for Jingzhou).
Shèng 賀拔勝 did not adopt his strategies,
abandoned the city, and fled to Liáng 梁.
Shúwǔ 叔武 returned to his home county,
built a house by the pond,
and lived a leisurely and content life.
Shìzōng 世宗 issued an imperial summons,
but he declined on grounds of illness and did not go.
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo 天保 era, he was again summoned,
and, having no choice,
he arrived in Yè 鄴 in a coarse robe, riding in an exposed carriage.
Yáng Yīn 楊愔 visited him
and appointed him Sītú Zīyì 司徒諮議 (Counselor to the Minister of Education),
but he claimed illness and refused the post.
Upon Sùzōng 肅宗’s ascension to the throne,
he was summoned to be Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ 太子中庶子 (Central Private Secretary to the Crown Prince)
and awarded the title Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū 銀青光祿大夫 (Grand Master of Silver and Blue Light).
When asked about state affairs,
Shúwǔ 叔武 advocated for attacking Guānxī 關西 (the region west of the Hangu Pass).
He drew a map and expounded on military strategy, saying:
“When the number of people and enemy forces are equal, one must rely on wisdom and strategy.
When wisdom and strategy are equal, one must rely on strength and power.
〔一一〕Thus, the strong control the weak,
and the rich absorb the poor.
Now, the Great Qí 大齊, compared to Guānxī 關西,
differs in strength and weakness,
and is unequal in wealth and poverty.
Yet, with constant warfare,
we have not been able to conquer and annex them.
This is a failure to utilize our strength and wealth.
Light troops engaging in open-field battles,
where victory and defeat are uncertain,
is the method of the Hú 胡 (nomadic cavalry),
not a well-thought-out, far-sighted, and foolproof strategy.
It is advisable to establish a strong fortress in Píngyáng 平陽,
opposite their Púzhōu 蒲州,
with deep moats and high ramparts.
Transport provisions and amass weapons,
and build garrison cities connected to it.
If they close their passes and do not come out,
then we seize their territory east of the Yellow River.
Cháng’ān 長安 will be greatly distressed
and naturally perish in its distress.
If they send out troops,
unless they number over one hundred thousand,
they will not be our match.
The provisions they supply
will all come from within the pass.
Our soldiers will rotate,
with a fresh contingent each year.
Our grain and food supplies will be abundant,
and transport will be uninterrupted.
If they come seeking battle,
we will not engage them.
If they retreat,
we will immediately exploit their weakness.
From Cháng’ān 長安 westward,
the population is sparse and cities are distant.
Enemy troops moving back and forth
will indeed face difficulties.
If they hold out against us,
agricultural work will cease.
In no more than three years,
they will collapse on their own.”
The emperor deeply accepted his proposal.
He also wished to reside in Píngyáng 平陽 himself
to realize this strategy.
The emperor ordered Yuán Wényáo 元文遙 to deliberate with Shúwǔ 叔武
and compile a volume on the “Strategy for Pacifying the West.”
Shortly after, the emperor died,
and the matter was consequently shelved.
When Shìzǔ 世祖 ascended the throne,
Shúwǔ 叔武 was appointed Yítóng Sānsī 儀同三司 (Honorary Administrator of the Three Ducal Offices) and Dūguān Shàngshū 都官尚書 (Minister of Population).
He was sent out as Hézhōu Cìshǐ 合州刺史 (Governor of Hezhou).
During the Wǔpíng 武平 era,
he was promoted to Tàizǐ Zhānshì 太子詹事 (Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince) and Yòuguānglù Dàfū 右光祿大夫 (Right Grand Master of Splendid Happiness).
When Shúwǔ 叔武 was in his hometown, he had a thousand *shi* 石 of grain.
Every spring and summer,
he would let villagers who had no food take it themselves,
and in autumn,
allowed them to repay at their discretion,
without keeping any accounts.
Yet, year after year, he always received more than double back.
Once he became an honored official at court,
he considered himself old,
and had many sons,
so he built a large house,
saying:
“We will sing here,
and weep here.”
Wèi Shōu 魏收 once came to visit him,
inquiring about old affairs in Luòjīng 洛京,
but left without waiting for food,
saying:
“It is hard to cause you expense.”
Shúwǔ 叔武 detained him.
After a long while, food arrived,
but it was only millet gruel and mallow greens,
served in wooden bowls,
with a single slice of dried meat.
His accompanying servants
were also served food,
exactly the same.
When Qí 齊 fell,
he returned to Fànyáng 范陽.
During the chaos, the city fell,
and Shúwǔ 叔武 and his cousin Shìsuì 士遂 both died of cold and hunger.
Zhōu 周 general Yǔwén Shénjǔ 宇文神舉, recognizing his renown and virtue,
collected and buried them.
Shúwǔ 叔武’s clan grandson, Chénkè 臣客,
was the son of Zǐguī 子規,
Wèi Shàngshū Láng 魏尚書郎 (Secretary to the Imperial Secretariat of Wei) and Línglǜ Jùnshǒu 林慮郡守 (Prefect of Linlü Commandery).
Chénkè 臣客 had a very fine demeanor,
had high aspirations in his youth,
was elegant and disciplined,
and fond of Daoist teachings.
His elder sister was the consort of Rènchéng Wáng 任城王.
At the end of the Tiānbǎo 天保 era,
Rènchéng Wáng 任城王 recommended him to the imperial court,
and he was consequently promoted to Tàizǐ Shèrén 太子舍人 (Attendant to the Crown Prince).
He was promoted to Sītú Jìshì 司徒記室 (Recorder for the Minister of Education),
but requested to return home to attend to his paternal grandmother, Lǐ 李.
Lǐ 李 urged him to serve,
and he reluctantly obeyed,
being appointed Tàizǐ Shèrén 太子舍人 and Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ 太子中庶子.
During the Wǔpíng 武平 era,
he concurrently served as Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍 (Palace Attendant Consultant) and was sent on an embassy to Chén 陳.
Upon his return,
he died on the road.
He was posthumously granted the titles Zhèngzhōu Cìshǐ 鄭州刺史 (Governor of Zhengzhou) and Hónglú Qīng 鴻臚卿 (Minister of the Court of Diplomatic Receptions).
Yáng Xiūzhī 陽休之,
courtesy name Zǐliè 子烈,
was a native of Wúzhōng 無終 in Yòuběipíng 右北平.
His father, Gù 固,
was Wèi Luòyáng Lìng 魏洛陽令 (Magistrate of Luoyang in Wei) and posthumously granted Tàicháng Shǎoqīng 太常少卿 (Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices).
Xiūzhī 休之 was intelligent, keen, and had a dignified bearing.
In his youth, he diligently studied
and loved refined literature.
He gained fame in his early twenties
as a rising talent.
Yōuzhōu Cìshǐ Cháng Jǐng 幽州刺史常景 and Wáng Yánnián 王延年 both summoned him to be Zhōuzhǔbù 州主簿 (Chief Clerk of the Prefecture).
During the Wèi Xiàochāng 魏孝昌 era,
Dù Luòzhōu 杜洛周 conquered Jìchéng 薊城.
Xiūzhī 休之, along with his clansmen and several thousand local families, fled south to Zhāngwǔ 章武,
then moved on to Qīngzhōu 青州.
At this time, Gé Róng 葛榮 was causing rebellion and chaos,
and many refugees from Héběi 河北 gathered in Qīngzhōu 青州.
Xiūzhī 休之 knew that a change was imminent,
so he asked his clan uncle Bóyàn 伯彥 and others, saying:
“The guest and host have different statuses,
and they are competing and insulting each other.
Disaster is about to break out.
In my humble opinion,
it is advisable to secretly return to the capital to avoid it.”
Most of them could not agree.
Xiūzhī 休之 tearfully took his leave.
Soon after, Xíng Gǎo 邢杲 rebelled,
and Bóyàn 伯彥 and others were all killed by the local populace.
〔一二〕Many perished at that time.
Dozens of the Yáng 陽 family died,
and only Xiūzhī 休之 and his brothers escaped.
When Emperor Zhuāngdì (莊帝) was enthroned,
he was appointed yuánwài sànqí shìláng (員外散騎侍郎) after doffing his coarse official robes.
Soon after, he was granted the additional duty of yùshǐ (御史) while retaining his original post.
He was promoted to gěishì zhōng (給事中) and tàiwèi jìshì cānjūn (太尉記室參軍),
and was granted the title of qīngchē jiāngjūn (輕車將軍).
Lǐ Shénjùn (李神儁), overseeing the "Diaries of Activity and Repose,"
memorialized that Xiūzhī (休之), along with Péi Bómào (裴伯茂) of Hédōng (河東), Lú Yuánmíng (盧元明) of Fànyáng (范陽), Xíng Zǐmíng (邢子明) of Héjiān (河間), and others, should be enlisted to compile and edit them.
At the end of the Yǒng'ān (永安) era,
Lǐ Hǎi (李海), the cìshǐ (刺史) of Luòzhōu (洛州), memorialized that he be appointed guānjūn chángshǐ (冠軍長史).
During the Pǔtài (普泰) period,
he concurrently held the post of tōngzhí sànqí shìláng (通直散騎侍郎),
was granted the title of zhènyuǎn jiāngjūn (鎮遠將軍),
and soon after became an assistant in the bureau of Zhǎngsūn Zhì (長孫稚), the tàibǎo (太保).
Soon, an imperial decree ordered him, along with Wèi Shōu (魏收), Lǐ Tóngguǐ (李同軌), and others, to compile the national history.
At the beginning of the Tàichāng (太昌) era,
he was appointed shàngshū cíwù lángzhōng (尚書祠部郎中),
and soon thereafter was promoted to zhēnglǔ jiāngjūn (征虜將軍) and zhōngsàn dàfū (中散大夫).
Hèbá Shèng (賀拔勝) was sent out as the cìshǐ (刺史) of Jīngzhōu (荊州),
and memorialized for Xiūzhī (休之) to be appointed piàojì chángshǐ (驃騎長史).
When Shèng (勝) became xíngtái (行臺),
he again requested Xiūzhī (休之) to be appointed yòuchéng (右丞).
When Shèng (勝) was strategizing in Fán (樊) and Miǎn (沔),
he again requested Xiūzhī (休zhī) to be appointed nándào jūnsī (南道軍司).
Shortly thereafter, Emperor Wǔdì (武帝) of Wèi (魏) entered Guānzhōng (關),
and Shèng (勝) ordered Xiūzhī (休之) to present a memorial and proceed to Cháng'ān (長安) for an audience.
At that time, Gāozǔ (高祖) also memorialized that Xiūzhī (休之) be appointed tàicháng shǎoqīng (太常少卿).
Soon, due to Shèng (勝) fleeing south,
he followed him to Jiànyè (建業).
When Xiūzhī (休之) heard that Gāozǔ (高祖) had elevated Emperor Jìngdì (靜帝),
he informed Shèng (勝) and requested Emperor Wǔ (武) of Liáng (梁) to allow him to return.
In the second year of Tiānpíng (天平), he reached Yè (鄴),
and then, by Gāozǔ (高祖)'s order, proceeded to Jìnyáng (晉陽).
In the winter of that year,
he was appointed kāifǔ zhǔbù (開府主簿) to Shìzōng (世宗).
In the spring of the following year,
when Shìzōng (世宗) became dàxíngtái (大行臺),
he was again appointed xíngtái lángzhōng (行臺郎中).
In the fourth year,
Gāozǔ (高祖) visited Tiānchí (天池) in Fényáng (汾陽).
By the side of the pond, a stone was found,
on which there was a raised inscription,
its text reading:
"Six kings, Three Rivers."
Gāozǔ (高祖) alone in his tent asked him,
"What is the meaning of this inscription?"
He replied:
"'Six' (六) refers to the character for 'king' (王) with an extra stroke,
meaning the great king (大王) is destined to rule the world.
This is an auspicious omen for the great king (大王) to receive the mandate.
Since this stone was found in Tiānchí (天池),
it can be said that Heaven has destined the king (王);
its auspiciousness cannot be expressed in words."
Gāozǔ (高祖) then asked, "What is the meaning of 'Three Rivers'?"
Xiūzhī (休之) replied:
"The Hé (河), Luò (洛), and Yī (伊) are the Three Rivers,
also referred to as the Jīng (涇), Wèi (渭), and Luò (洛) as the Three Rivers.
The Hé (河), Luò (洛), and Yī (伊) refer to
Luòyáng (洛陽);
the Jīng (涇), Wèi (渭), and Luò (洛) refer to
the present Yōngzhōu (雍州).
If the great king (大王) receives the Mandate of Heaven,
he will eventually control Guānyòu (關右)."
Gāozǔ (高祖) said:
"People often say without cause that I wish to rebel.
Now hearing this,
it will cause even more controversy.
Be careful not to speak carelessly."
At the beginning of the Yuánxiàng (元象) era,
for his military achievements in Jīngzhōu (荊州),
he was enfeoffed as the founding count (kāiguó bó 郡國伯) of Xīntài County (新泰縣),
with an income of six hundred households.
He was appointed píngdōng jiāngjūn (平東將軍), tàizhōng dàfū (太中大夫), and shàngshū zuǒ mín lángzhōng (尚書左民郎中).
In the second year of Xīnghé (興和),
he concurrently held the post of tōngzhí sànqí chángshì (通直散騎常侍),
and accompanied Cuī Chángqiān (崔長謙) of Qīnghé (清河) as an envoy to Liáng (梁).
In the second year of Wǔdìng (武定),
he was appointed zhōngshū shìláng (中書侍郎).
At that time, a scholar playfully ridiculed Xiūzhī (休之), saying:
"There is a ram with horns entangled in a fence,
riding a dappled horse with a chain pattern,
traveling from Jìnyáng (晉陽) to Yè (鄴),
carrying a handful of letters."
Lú Fěi (盧斐), shàngshū zuǒchéng (尚書左丞), requested an audience with these documents,
and memorialized Gāozǔ (高祖) to prohibit such behavior.
However, he was pardoned and not punished.
In the fifth year,
he concurrently served as shàngshí diǎnyù (尚食典御).
In the seventh year,
he was appointed tàizǐ zhōngshùzǐ (太子中庶子),
promoted to gěishì huángmén shìláng (給事黃門侍郎),
and granted the titles of zhōngjūn jiāngjūn (中軍將軍) and Yōuzhōu dàzhōngzhèng (幽州大中正).
In the eighth year,
he concurrently served as shìzhōng (侍中),
and bearing credentials, went with imperial decrees sealed with a jade seal to Bīngzhōu (幷州),
to persuade Xiǎnzǔ (顯祖) to accept the positions of xiàngguó (相國) and Qíwáng (齊王).
At this time,
Xiǎnzǔ (顯祖) was about to receive the abdication from Wèi (魏).
He departed from Jìnyáng (晉陽),
and reached Píngyáng Commandery (平陽郡),
but as people's sentiments were not yet unified,
he returned to Bīngzhōu (幷州).
Fearing a leak,
he then blocked travelers.
Xiūzhī (休之) was naturally loose-tongued.
Upon his return from the mission,
he recounted the matter,
and everyone in Yè (鄴) knew about it.
Later, Gāo Dézhèng (高德政) heard about it and reported it,
and Xiǎnzǔ (顯祖) was furious but did not act immediately.
When Qí (齊) received the abdication,
he was appointed sànqí chángshì (散騎常侍),
and compiled the "Diaries of Activity and Repose."
A short while later,
he was demoted to xiāojì jiāngjūn (驍騎將軍) for an error in an imperial decree,
this being cumulative with previous incidents.
Soon after, due to his participation in settling the rites and ceremonies during the abdication,
he was separately enfeoffed as the founding baron (kāiguó nán 開國男) of Shǐpíng County (始平縣),
and concurrently held the position of lǐngjūn sīmǎ (領軍司馬) with his original rank.
Later, he was appointed dūshuǐ shǐzhě (都水使者),
served as sīhú yuán (司徒掾) and zhōngshū shìláng (中書侍郎),
and soon after was appointed zhòngshān tàishǒu (中山太守).
When Xiǎnzǔ (顯祖) passed away,
Xiūzhī (休之) was summoned to Jìnyáng (晉陽)
to oversee the funeral arrangements.
In the first year of Gānmíng (乾明),
he concurrently served as shìzhōng (侍中)
to inspect the capital and its environs.
He was then appointed dàhónglú qīng (大鴻臚卿),
and concurrently held zhōngshū shìláng (中書侍郎).
At the beginning of Huángjiàn (皇建),
with his original rank, he concurrently held dùzhī shàngshū (度支尚書),
was granted the title of piàojì dàjiāngjūn (驃騎大將軍),
and concurrently served as Yōuzhōu dàzhōngzhèng (幽州大中正).
Sùzōng (肅宗) paid close attention to governance,
and frequently consulted Xiūzhī (休之) on administrative methods.
Xiūzhī (休之) responded that clear rewards and punishments,
careful appointment of officials,
prohibiting extravagance,
and caring for the people's suffering were the priorities of governance.
The Emperor greatly accepted his advice.
During the Dàníng (大寧) era,
he was appointed dūguān shàngshū (都官尚書),
and then transferred to qībīng (七兵) and cíwù (祠部).
In the third year of Héqīng (河清),
he was sent out as the cìshǐ (刺史) of Xīyǎnlüzhōu (西兗州).
At the beginning of Tiāntǒng (天統),
he was summoned back as guānglù qīng (光祿卿),
and supervised the national history.
While Xiūzhī (休之) served in Zhōngshān (中山) and governed Xīyǎnlü (西兗),
he implemented benevolent policies in both places,
and was cherished by the officials and people.
After leaving office,
the common people erected steles to praise his virtues.
Soon after, he was appointed lìbù shàngshū (吏部尚書),
received salary from Yángwǔ County (陽武縣),
was appointed yítóng sānsī (儀同三司),
and was also granted the title of kāifǔ (開府).
Xiūzhī (休之) was knowledgeable about historical precedents
and familiar with clans.
All those he selected and appointed
were invariably talented and suitable for their positions.
He was granted the title of jīnzǐ guānglù dàfū (金紫光祿大夫).
In the first year of Wǔpíng (武平),
he was appointed zhōngshū jiān (中書監),
and soon after concurrently held shàngshū yòupúyè (尚書右僕射) with his original rank.
In the second year,
he was granted the title of zuǒ guānglù dàfū (左光祿大夫),
and concurrently held zhōngshū jiān (中書監).
In the third year,
he was granted the title of tèjìn (特進).
In the fifth year,
he was officially appointed zhōngshū jiān (中書監),
with all other titles remaining as before.
Soon after, due to old age, he retired from office,
presenting a memorial to resign his position.
The Emperor graciously responded but did not permit it.
In the sixth year,
he was officially appointed shàngshū yòupúyè (尚書右僕射).
Not long after,
he again concurrently held zhōngshū jiān (中書監).
